facts.value: CS HCP students enroll in 3-7 units each autumn, winter and spring; summer is optional. The 45-unit degree must be completed within five years, usually in 3-5 years. US residence is required. The dedicated HCP page specifies HB1 (as written) for international students, whereas the general MS page says they must be employed and located in the US. AI, Information Management and Analytics, and Systems specializations can be completed online; others require campus courses. Tuition is per unit. Campus housing and campus employment are unavailable. Request a status change at least three weeks before the quarter; at most two changes (one round trip) are allowed.
conditions: Confirm international visa eligibility with CS or CGOE before treating general US employment as sufficient; the official pages use inconsistent wording.

scope.cycle: Current route rules; exact applicationterms separately dated

facts.value: MSE HCP requires US residence; its page specifies an H1B visa for international students. Complete 45 units within five years. Enroll in 3-7 units each autumn, winter and spring, including at least three units applicable to the degree; summer is optional. MSE courses are in person; only approved electives in other departments may be online. Campus housing and employment are unavailable. A full-time-to-HCP transfer is discretionary and must be requested at least three weeks before the quarter. Coterm students can transfer only after bachelor degree conferral. At most two enrollment-status changes are allowed. The degree and admission criteria match the full-time MS.
conditions: HCP is not an online-only MSE degree.

scope.cycle: Current route rules; exact applicationterms separately dated

facts.value: ME HCP serves local working professionals and cannot be completed entirely online. Its application uses the regular process. All three recommendations and required materials must arrive by the deadline; extensions and changes to submitted materials are not allowed. A completed or enrolled related MS excludes another ME MS application; an unrelated MS may be acceptable. PhD applicants without an MS may receive rare automatic MS consideration after a PhD denial. Admission deferral is reviewed only for exceptional circumstances, such as military service or medical issues.
conditions: FAQ dates/GREcutoffs remain 2025-26; currentprogramdeadline/GREcomesfrom 2027 directory and updatedadmissionpage, not FAQhistoricaldates.

scope.cycle: Current route rules; exact applicationterms separately dated

facts.value: EE HCP students typically take 3-6 units per quarter and finish 45 units in 3-5 years. Online completion depends on the program plan and available courses. Admission is autumn only. Part-time students working full-time receive no departmental aid; employer reimbursement may be available. Up to 18 NDO units may count, but credits from another institution cannot transfer. Applicants already holding an EE MS may apply if they explain their reasons. Industry recommendations are accepted, although academic letters are preferred. Transfer from part-time to full-time requires at least two completed non-summer quarters and 15 letter-graded lecture or lab units. A GPA of at least 3.5 is expected for that request. Transfer in the final degree quarter is not permitted; at most two changes are allowed and approval is discretionary.
conditions: The GPA of 3.5 is an expectation for a later enrollment-status transfer, not an initial HCP admission minimum.

scope.cycle: Current route rules; exact applicationterms separately dated

facts.value: CEE regular MS students may request HCP status for part-time work or internships. Online course availability depends on the subplan; no regular CEE MS can be completed entirely online, and Atmosphere/Energy courses are in person. PhD students and international students holding a student visa are ineligible for this regular HCP status. HCP students cannot receive university assistantships or fellowships and cannot live in student housing. A return to full-time status restores eligibility to apply for housing. At most two status changes are allowed. Up to 18 qualifying NDO units may count after the first graduate quarter.
conditions: Hybrid SES has separate international and residential-phase rules; do not apply the regular HCP student-visa restriction to its overseas online phase.

scope.cycle: Current route rules; exact applicationterms separately dated

facts.value: Hybrid SES is a 45-unit CEE MS configuration. The initial third of the degree is part-time online study at 3-7 units per quarter, typically over 3-6 quarters, followed by three full-time campus quarters. Typical total duration is 2-3 years. Its four depth areas are structures and materials, sustainable construction, environmental engineering, and atmosphere and energy. Systems and data courses, depth courses, electives and a breadth experience are required. GRE, a minimum admission GPA, a prior CEE major and specific admission coursework are not required. Applicants with an existing MS are eligible if they explain their reasons. Up to 18 NDO units may count; other-institution transfer credit cannot. International applicants may apply from overseas, but student visas are issued only for the full-time campus phase. Housing is available only in that phase. KHS is unavailable, and working part-time students receive no departmental aid; admission carries no funding guarantee. CGOE bills the HCP phase and Student Services bills the residential phase. Students cannot interchange the curriculum or transfer to the ordinary residential MS; PhD study requires a new application.
conditions: The hybrid admission FAQ still rejects IELTS, while the current general CEE and central Graduate Admissions pages accept it. Confirm English-test acceptance for the hybrid route before assessment.
The exact hybrid application window and per-unit price remain researched unknowns. A generic CEE deadline or ordinary full-time tuition bracket cannot silently replace them.

facts.value: Current Stanford students applying to a new CS MS or PhD use the ordinary application and external applicant requirements; CS does not accept general added-degree GAP petitions. The separately documented same-program CS PhD-to-MS progression is an exception and must not be mistaken for an open other-department MS petition.

Existing CS PhD students without an MSCS may petition after faculty alignment, foundation/breadth and candidacy. Existing coterm must be withdrawn first. GAP fee is USD 125; petition before application-to-graduate deadline and at least one quarter before MS conferral. Conferral additionally requires qualifying exam, 45 units and GPA 3.0. Up to 45 units from Stanford MS or external graduate study count to PhD residence; combining Stanford MS with any external transfer raises PhD residency from 135 to 180 units.
conditions: Degree GPA and qualifying milestones are post-admission progress requirements.

facts.value: CS MS/MBA requires separate CS and GSB admission; apply concurrently or during first year of either. Second-year CS or MBA students may not join. CS JD/MS requires separate admission and both-unit consent; Law entrants apply concurrently or no later than earlier of end of Law year 2 and following-year CS deadline. First Law year is full-time Law; cross-counted courses need both schools approval. CS JD/PhD requires separate admission, supervising faculty contact and both-unit permission; enrolled students may apply to other program after starting.
conditions: MBA and JD/MS restrictions apply only to their named joint configuration, not ordinary external CS degree admission.

facts.value: ICME PhD good-standing support lasts the program under department standard; individual package arrives with admission. Selective SGF auto-consideration gives quarterly stipend and 8-10 unit tuition for 12 quarters(three years); Engineering/department fellowships give some entrants stipend+8-10 units up to 4 first-yearquarters. MS has no funding guarantee.50 percent RA/TA typically covers 8-10 units plus salary for 20 hours/week; lesser appointments adjust benefits. RA is faculty-arranged; CA application is on ICME intranet and TA orientation required. Funding page has old 2024 KHS date; use current separately sourced 2027 KHS timing.
conditions: Department-standard individual amounts and future stipend values remain offer-specific; no universal MS funding.

facts.value: University minimum for most master’s programs: 45 Stanford units, all 100-level or above, with at least 50% primarily for graduate students (typically 200-level+). Coterminal candidates have three years from first graduate quarter. Program requirements may exceed these minima.

facts.value: Individually Designed MA in Education is intended for current Stanford doctoral students in a PhD outside GSE. Admission follows GSE consultation and an individualized plan; complete 45 units including at least 27 GSE units within three years, then file Graduate Authorization Petition.
conditions: Not an external entry route.

facts.value: GSE takes a limited number of Stanford undergraduates into MA/MS coterm study after at least 120 units toward graduation; undergraduate department approval and GSE admission both required.

GSE MA specializations include Curriculum and Teacher Education, Global and Comparative Education, International Education Policy Analysis, Policy, Organization and Leadership Studies, plus joint MA/MBA, MA/JD and MA/MPP. MS offerings include Education Data Science and Learning, Design, and Technology. STEP is a 12-month MA with preliminary California credential; GSE also lists Teaching of Physics MA.
conditions: Bulletin award rows group specializations; current admissions route must be checked per track.

facts.value: For 2027-28 entry, GSE PhD deadline is November 16, 2026; MA/MS deadline is January 7, 2027. Knight-Hennessy applicants to GSE must separately meet the November 16, 2026 KHS program deadline.

GRE is not required for 2027-28; applicants may submit optional scores without penalty. Applicants not meeting the central English exemption must meet GSE minimum TOEFL iBT 100 before Jan 21 2026 or 5 after that date, or IELTS Academic 7.5.

Core GSE application asks for 1-2 page single-spaced 12-point statement of purpose, resume/CV, three recommendations, and transcripts from every college/university attended at least one full-time academic year. Upload PDFs/scanned records; current in-progress transcript accepted before degree conferral. Foreign-language transcripts need complete literal translation; admitted students later send official records.
conditions: The general Education MA option represents shared ordinary GSE MA guidance only. STEP, individually designed MA, closed CTE intake and joint GSB/Law/POLS-forwarded routes use their own application instructions. Selecting a named variant must not inherit this checklist by parent degree alone.

facts.value: Doctoral program committees may interview. Writing sample is not required for CTE, DAPS, LSTD, or Economics of Education; required 10+ page research-oriented samples for Anthropology of Education, Educational Linguistics, History of Education, Global and Comparative Education, Philosophy of Education; required research samples for EDS, Higher Education, Sociology of Education and RILE. LSTD and RILE applicants under SHIPS must apply to that area and another SHIPS subplan. RILE sample topic must relate to race, inequality and/or language; 1,000-5,000 words preferred. The History/Social Science Education PhD area will not admit for 2027-28.
conditions: Some area committees may interview; others state no interview.

facts.value: DAPS, Economics of Education, Education Data Science, Educational Policy, Higher Education, and Sociology of Education specify supplemental essays/skills questions; respond to each area-specific prompt on the GSE page.

For 2027-28: CTE MA will not admit. EDS MS has no writing sample or interview but requires supplemental essays/skills matrix and basic programming experience/coursework; LDT MS has no writing sample/interview and uses a program-specific statement and short answers. GCE/IEPA MA requires an English research writing sample of at least 10 pages and track-specific statement. POLS MA requires a writing sample up to 10 pages and supplemental essays.
conditions: CTE closure applies to the stated 2027-28 cycle only.

facts.value: STEP applicants choose Elementary or one of five Secondary subject areas (English, history/social science, math, science, world languages). The 12-month full-time program leads to MA plus preliminary California teaching credential. STEP requires a 750-1,250 word essay (max 3 pages), resume, three recommendations, and transcripts for each institution attended at least one year. Current page contains inconsistent 2026-27/2027 cohort term references; follow current application and the 2027-28 MA deadline.
conditions: The historical cycle/start-term mismatch needs live application confirmation.

facts.value: MFA applicants submit an online SlideRoom portfolio by deadline; $10 SlideRoom fee. Include typed work list with date, medium, size, title and viewing instructions. Still-image total max 20; time-based selection max 10 minutes (preferred excerpt 5 minutes). SOP no more than two pages; first sentence must name program and area. Three references, postsecondary transcripts for each full-time institution attended at least one academic year. GRE not required; department states TOEFL for applicants whose first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted, while current central exemptions apply.
conditions: Art & Art History page says TOEFL is required when the applicant’s first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted; central Graduate Admissions lists TOEFL or IELTS and exemptions. Confirm which stricter rule the Art Practice application currently enforces.

facts.value: Autumn-only entry, December 1 at 9 p.m. Pacific deadline; all materials including tests/recommendations/portfolio must arrive by deadline. Department normally provides support package through fellowship plus teaching assistantships, including tuition support, salary and small materials grants; two-year full-time program, typically admits up to five yearly.
conditions: Finalists must travel to Stanford for late-February faculty/student interview. Funding wording is typical/normal rather than guaranteed individual award.

facts.value: Submit one 5-8 page analytical essay on a documentary film/topic as PDF; submit SlideRoom portfolio with film/video work where applicant had creative control if possible. Total sample runtime max 15 minutes, with synopsis, clip runtime and applicant role; minimal production experience may be represented by strongest work in another visual medium. No production-assistant-only work. SlideRoom fee is $6. SOP max two pages; three recommendations and transcripts for institutions attended full-time for at least one year.

Autumn 2027-28 application materials due December 1 at 9 p.m. Pacific; no midyear entry. Two consecutive years in residence. First year fellowship includes stipend and tuition; second-year TA eligibility includes salary and tuition allowance. Production funds also offered.
conditions: Second-year TA support is eligibility, not guaranteed award.

facts.value: Music PhD/DMA applicants must hold a bachelor’s degree; PhD/DMA applicants are expected to have preparation equivalent to a Music bachelor’s. Terminal MA Music, Science, and Technology targets applicants with undergraduate engineering, science, music, arts, or a degree including engineering mathematics. Application requires SOP, three recommendations, unofficial transcripts for each school attended at least one year; MA/PhD also require scholarly writing sample. DMA composition adds complete composition list and links to representative scores and 3-6 audio/video recordings.

GRE is optional for all Music graduate programs. Application for September entry opens late September/early October; completed application due the second Tuesday in December. TOEFL is required for international applicants whose primary language is not English unless they meet waiver requirements. Department does not provide its own fee waiver.
conditions: Program-specific 2027 cycle deadline is in the central directory; department page describes second-Tuesday rule.

facts.value: Doctoral-level Music applicants are expected to have preparation equivalent to a bachelor’s in Music; department suggests comparing prior study to Stanford Music bachelor’s requirements to identify missing theory/history preparation. After admission, incoming doctoral students take dictation and theory diagnostics; musicologists/composers take piano proficiency; ethnomusicologists take piano/other instrument proficiency or non-Western musical traditions test; musicologists take Western-art-music history/repertoire test. Deficiencies may delay TA assignment until remedied.

The terminal History MA is for students who do not intend to continue into Stanford History’s PhD; admitted terminal MA students may not apply to enter the department PhD while working on the MA. Autumn-only entry. Apply through central graduate application with statement of purpose, three recommendations, scanned transcripts for every college attended at least one year, and a 10-25 page history writing sample. GRE general is not required; confirm English testing against central 2027-28 rules. 2027-28 application deadline is December 1, 2026.
conditions: Department page states “11:59 p.m. EST” while central application deadline instructions state 11:59 p.m. Pacific; rely on the live application deadline screen for submission timezone.

facts.value: History MA candidates, terminal and coterminal, receive no departmental funding; any separately awarded university-wide scholarship is not established by this source.

scope.cycle: 2026-2027 Spring and 2027-2028 Autumn terms as separately published

facts.value: History admits a limited number of Stanford undergraduates to the coterm MA. Applicants specify a field and faculty advisor and need 3.75 GPA in History courses (or equivalent preparation if not a History major). Requirements include coterm application, statement, Stanford transcript, 10-25 page history sample, three recommendations (at least two from History faculty; one from current advisor and one from prospective MA advisor), preliminary program proposal and course-transfer information. Spring-quarter entry only; 2026-27 deadline December 1, 2026. Courses cannot double-count toward both degrees.
conditions: Coterm admissions are an internal undergraduate route and must not be treated as external terminal admission.

facts.value: History guarantees five years of continuous 12-month funding for doctoral students who remain actively enrolled and in good academic standing. Package combines fellowship and assistantship support and provides tuition, stipend/salary, summer stipend and health insurance. Students may separately apply for relocation, conference-travel and research grants.
conditions: Five-year guarantee has active-enrollment and good-standing conditions.

facts.value: EALC applicants need at least three years of training in the language of intended specialization; a prior EALC undergraduate major is not required. Applicants must seek graduate study in a scholarly field (e.g., literature/culture, linguistics, archaeology or Trans-Asian studies), not merely language acquisition.

EALC MA requires a research/writing sample of approximately 15 pages and three recommendations; applicants upload transcripts and the department may contact finalists for Zoom interviews. Students normally complete 45 units and enroll in at least 8 units each quarter. EALC provides limited tuition fellowships to admitted MA students and encourages outside funding.
conditions: Three recommendations, writing sample and transcript requirements apply to the EALC MA route.

facts.value: EALC offers five years of 12-month PhD funding through fellowship, research-assistantship and teaching-assistantship support; students are encouraged to seek outside fellowships.

Comparative Literature PhD: scholarly literary-critical/analytic sample about 5,000 words in English; creative writing is not a substitute. French and Italian graduate programs: two 20-page samples, one in English and one in French or Italian. German Studies: approximately 5,000 words of scholarly analysis in German or English. Iberian and Latin American Cultures: two 20-page samples, one English and one Spanish. Slavic Languages and Literatures: about 20 pages in English analyzing Slavic texts; a short Russian or other relevant-language sample is optional.

Slavic PhD students are required to learn/read Russian, one quarter of Old Church Slavonic, and at least two other languages relevant to research (often French, German or another Slavic language, with alternatives depending on research interests).

Classics PhD application asks for an academic paper in the field, 15-25 pages, and a CV listing language qualifications; ancient-language preparation should be demonstrated by works read in the original and modern-language proficiency may be described by level and years studied. The department says a strong Classics or related-field background is expected.
conditions: Department page’s English-test wording should be reconciled with current university exemption and accepted-test policy.

facts.value: English PhD deadline is December 1, 2026. Submit a critical/scholarly writing sample 12-25 pages (excluding references), preferably in intended area and clear of grading comments. Statement should ideally be 500-600 words and may not exceed 1,000 words.

The 2026-27 Bulletin has a Classics MA degree row, while the Classics Graduate Admissions page states that its MA has been discontinued. The current external directory does not list a Classics MA entry.
conditions: The official current admissions page says discontinued.

facts.value: The application originates with GSB MBA Admissions. Applicants select interest in the joint program in the MBA application and complete an additional essay. Current MBA1 students may apply during their first quarter using the internal joint application. The program is two years full-time.

Apply through the GSE POLS MA application, indicate MA/MPP consideration and complete the joint-degree prompt. If admitted to POLS, GSE forwards the application to Public Policy; POLS admission is required, but MPP admission is separate. Econ 1 and Math 20 are required before matriculation, though not necessarily at application.
conditions: Both programs try to issue concurrent decisions, but timing may differ; final decisions precede April 15.

facts.value: Applicants may apply through the Law School and indicate joint MA/JD interest, or apply after Law School admission before the earlier of the end of JD year two or the GSE deadline for the intended MA start. Both schools must approve the joint course of study.

The History of Art MA is only available to Art & Art History PhD students as progress toward the PhD. The department does not admit students who want only the MA. The PhD field may include Film & Media Studies; doctoral students also complete collateral studies in another graduate department or interdisciplinary program.

Submit three recommendation letters; scanned transcripts for each postsecondary institution attended full-time for at least one academic year; and an SOP of no more than 1,000 words, single spaced, 12-point Times New Roman, 1-inch margins, naming the PhD program and field in its first sentence. One writing sample of at most 20 pages including illustrations and bibliography; full master’s theses are not accepted. GRE is not required. Finalists may be interviewed by faculty via Skype. Autumn-only admission; department page gives December 1, 9 p.m. Pacific deadline and decisions around March 15.
conditions: Department page says TOEFL required when first language is not English and IELTS is not accepted; reconcile with central university policy and exemption criteria.
exceptions: Department deadline page says 9 p.m. Pacific while central Graduate Admissions permits submission by 11:59 p.m. Pacific; verify the stricter department cutoff in live application.

facts.value: Art History PhD normally has a five-year support package from departmental fellowships, teaching and research assistantships; additional support includes summer language study, summer research, and individual research/travel funds. Students select a particular art-history field (including Film & Media Studies), complete collateral graduate study; progress review occurs at end of year two, dissertation topic/proposal by end of year three, and dissertation must be completed within five years after candidacy.
conditions: Support is described as normal rather than a guaranteed award; candidacy completion starts a separate five-year dissertation clock.

facts.value: For 2027-28 GSE coterm entry, Stanford undergraduates need at least 120 units toward graduation, apply to one coterm program per term, and submit the coterm application, preliminary program proposal, statement of purpose, resume, undergraduate transcript and two recommendations. GRE is not required. Deadline January 7, 2027; decisions in early March; accepted applicants respond by April 15, 2027 before completion of their undergraduate degree. The CTE MA accepts no applications for this cycle.

GSE masters programs are largely self-funded. The 2026-27 published cost-of-attendance page gives program-specific budgets for GCE/IEPA, LDT, POLS and EDS; EDS year-two 2027-28 figures are estimates. No one school-wide price applies to STEP or the joint degrees. All domestic and international applicants are automatically considered for Deans Fellowships; the award is included with the admission offer if granted and is final. Zaentz fellowship consideration for EDS, GCE/IEPA, LDT and POLS requires separate early-childhood responses in the online application.

GSE offers all admitted Education PhD students a five-year package of tuition aid, fellowship stipend and assistantship salary covering the standard cost of attendance for the student alone. Assistantship work is part of the package; this is not a funding promise for GSE masters or joint-degree applicants.

Education Data Science MS is a two-year full-time residential program with at least 51 units. It combines coursework in education and data science with an internship and mentored original research projects; its duration and cost cannot be inferred from the one-year MA/MS tracks.

Global and Comparative Education and International Education Policy Analysis are two tracks of a 48-unit MA. Both complete an MA research paper through the EDUC 206 series; GCE and IEPA have distinct track requirements. The program includes summer enrollment.

Learning Design and Technology MS requires at least 45 units, including at least 30 GSE units, over the academic year and summer. It includes internship workshops in at least two quarters, a learning portfolio and a masters design project.

Policy, Organization and Leadership Studies MA requires at least 45 units, including at least 27 GSE units, across Autumn through Spring. Its 2026-27 field placement involves about 150 hours and a project deliverable.

STEP Secondary admits by the intended credential subject: English, history/social science, mathematics, science or world languages. Candidates complete at least 45 units over four quarters, student teaching alongside coursework, an Education MA and a preliminary California single-subject teaching credential.

The Division of Literatures, Cultures, and Languages states all admitted PhD students receive five years of 12-month funding through tuition/fellowship and research or teaching assistantships; its programs do not provide financial support to masters students. Division departments do not grant their own application fee waivers; applicants may review central university waiver routes. The division page currently labels its admission cycle ambiguously, so no deadline is inferred here.

English PhD admits receive five years of 12-month support through fellowship and assistantships, with non-guaranteed sixth-year consideration. PhD candidates demonstrate reading knowledge of one foreign language; the department prefers evidence before admission. Teaching includes a first-year pedagogy seminar and typically three teaching assignments.

Modern Thought and Literature PhD requests a purpose statement no longer than 1,500 words explaining interdisciplinary preparation and a scholarly critical/analytic writing sample of at most 7,000 words; creative writing is not a substitute. No particular undergraduate major is required. Admitted students receive a five-year plan covering tuition and stipend/salary, including five summers.

The Modern Thought and Literature coterm MA is for current Stanford undergraduates well prepared in literature and at least one foreign language, including students from other majors. Its application asks for a roughly 20-page analytical writing sample and is due January 13, 2027.

Religious Studies PhD applicants specify a field, provide an SOP of at most five double-spaced pages, three confidential recommendations, transcripts and a 15-25 page double-spaced English academic writing sample on religion preceded by a short rationale. GRE is optional. Faculty consider prior religious-studies and research-language preparation and fit with faculty resources. Decisions normally arrive late February; offers may be accepted through April 15.

Religious Studies PhD students are eligible for up to five years of funding, including tuition, student Cardinal Care insurance, stipend or teaching assistantships, plus up to five funded summers. The department does not fund coterminal or masters students.

East Asian Studies MA 2027-28 application closes December 3, 2026. External applicants select Humanities/Social Sciences method and China/Japan/Korea region; submit transcripts, three recommendations, purpose statement (recommended at most 1,000 words), and first 15 double-spaced pages of an English academic nonfiction writing sample. GRE is not considered. CEAS offers limited fellowships, contingent on availability; check yes for financial aid in the application. Coterm applicants have different recommendation requirements and are considered for CEAS fellowships only under stated enrollment rules.

Russian, East European and Eurasian Studies MA application deadline is January 12, 2027. External terminal and current Stanford undergraduate coterm applications use separate online routes. External applicants submit transcripts, an at-most-two-page purpose statement, three relevant faculty references (one preferably language instructor), a writing sample of no more than 20 English pages and a list of relevant coursework with grades. Three years of relevant language study is strong preparation, but candidates with less are considered; this is not a hard minimum.

Latin American Studies MA requires Spanish at B1 CEFR/intermediate-high ACTFL or equivalent third-year university study and experience studying, working or living in Latin America/Iberia. External applicants provide a short purpose statement, 150-250 word proposed-research abstract, English academic writing sample and Spanish-fluency statement where their degree was not at a Spanish-language institution. Current Stanford undergraduates may use the coterm route after 120 units. Department fellowships and assistantships are competitive/available rather than guaranteed; applicants indicate aid interest in the online application.

Theater and Performance Studies accepts external PhD applications only, not a terminal MA. It asks for a purpose statement (at most two double-spaced pages), artistic statement (at most three), production-experience summary/CV, one or two scholarly papers totaling no more than 25 pages, transcripts and three recommendations. GRE is not required; a masters is not required. Applicants may be interviewed; decisions are communicated in March. The current official Graduate Admissions directory corroborates the November 24, 2026 deadline in the page header; the body still contains a stale November 25, 2025 date.

Theater and Performance Studies PhD describes a five-year fellowship package with tuition, health insurance, travel award and living stipend. First years emphasize full-time study; later years include teaching and dissertation writing.

Music DMA and PhD doctoral students receive five years of 12-month funding; individual Cardinal Care premiums are covered for three academic quarters in each of the five years. Later assistantships depend on department needs. The Music, Science, and Technology terminal MA does not typically receive department or center funding, although an eligible student may occasionally receive fellowship or teaching support; no award is assured. The department offers no departmental application fee waiver.

Classics PhD offers a six-year funding package conditional on satisfactory progress. Through year five the package provides stipend, tuition and health insurance for four academic quarters per year; it includes five funded summers. Applicants do not file a separate departmental funding application.

The MLA is a part-time, on-campus evening program normally lasting four or five years, with at least 50 units and an interdisciplinary thesis. Most students take one course per quarter. MLA students are not eligible for Stanford graduate housing.

The currently available MLA tuition page quotes $12,708 annual tuition for 2025-26, billed in three installments, with separate document and student-activity fees. This is historical for a 2027 applicant, not a current-cycle quote. Admission is need-blind; the MLA tuition-assistance program seeks to help students with demonstrated need after admission. Part-time MLA students generally lack traditional student-loan eligibility.

For 2027 entry, GSE plans PhD decisions in mid-February and masters/coterm decisions in early March. Responses are due April 15, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. Pacific. STEP begins June 21, 2027; other GSE PhD and masters programs begin September 20, 2027. These dates are GSE routes, not joint MBA/JD decisions.

STEP candidates need a bachelors degree before program start. California subject-matter competence may be shown through CSET, qualifying coursework, aligned degree, or approved preparation program; at least half the subject domains are due by program start and all CSET subtests by August. A foreign bachelors degree requires approved equivalency evaluation for California basic-skills credential purposes. The STEP page mixes old cohort dates; verify calendar-specific test deadlines for 2027.

STEP offers need/merit tuition fellowships of $5,000-$35,000 and a small number of full-tuition Stanford Teaching Fellows awards. Qualified future teachers may receive a forgivable loan up to $40,000 tied to teaching at an eligible U.S. school, with half forgiven after two years and the balance after four. Applicants seeking these fellowships complete the STEP supplemental funding section and FAFSA; no award is automatic.

Biology and Biophysics are two of 14 Stanford Biosciences PhD Home Programs spanning Humanities and Sciences and Medicine. They use the shared Biosciences application for Autumn 2027-28, due December 1, 2026 at 11:59:59 p.m. PST. GRE General is not considered for either; Biology does not consider a GRE Subject test, while Biophysics treats Mathematics or Physics Subject scores as optional. The applicant selects a Home Program; these two H&S awards should not be reclassified as School of Medicine awards.

Linguistics accepts only currently enrolled Stanford undergraduates to its coterm MA, not external MA applicants. For Spring 2026-27 entry, application deadline is January 12, 2027. Submit Stanford transcript, purpose statement explaining the MA and possible research paper, adviser-approved program proposal, named Linguistics faculty adviser, and three references including one Linguistics faculty member.

value.A3i6E: The study of Classics has traditionally centered on the literature and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome, including Greek and Latin language, literature, philosophy, history, art, and archaeology. At Stanford, Classics also explores connections with other ancient cultures and the modern world, as well as specialized fields such as ancient economics, law, papyrology, and science. The department’s faculty approaches Classics from an interdisciplinary perspective that crosses geographical, temporal, and thematic territories. Studying ancient epic poetry can lead to looking at modern cinema afresh; ancient Athenian politics opens new perspectives on contemporary politics; and the study of Rome presents parallels with other empires just as Latin illuminates the history of English and the Romance languages. In short, Classics at Stanford is an interdisciplinary subject concerned not only with Greek and Roman civilization but also with the interaction of cultures and societies that influenced the ancient Mediterranean basin and continue to influence human society across the globe. The MA in Classics is no longer accepting new students. The last admit date for this program was Spring 2024. This program is only available for current Classics-PhD students. Please see the Student Services Officer for further information.
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Classics is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. The goal of advising in the graduate program is to help students select courses that best suit their intellectual pursuits, design and conduct research, navigate degree requirements, explore academic and professional opportunities, and prepare for their postgraduate careers. Graduate students are expected to be active collaborators in the advising relationship. They are responsible for seeking academic and professional guidance and informing themselves of the MA program’s policies and degree requirements. An essential part of the advisee-advisor relationship is for students to discuss their expectations for the adviser-advisee relationship with the advisor and revisit these expectations periodically. Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) A Department faculty member is the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS). The DGS monitors the degree progress of all MA and PhD students, offers advice on meeting department and university requirements, coordinates departmental advising and Teaching Assistant (TA) assignments, and approves petitions for funding or other needs before submission to the Graduate Committee (see below). Track Advisor MA students are admitted to one of four tracks within the Classics Department, each with its own requirements (Archaeology, History, Literature, and Philosophy). Each track also has an individual advisor in the pre-dissertation stage, advising on track-specific coursework, training in research methodologies, and professional development. Entering students should meet routinely (at least once per quarter) with both the DGS and the track advisor, who approve a course of study, monitor progress, and provide advice about funding opportunities, strategies for scheduling general and other exams required for degree progress, and to provide support if difficulties arise. Student Services Officer (SSO) In addition, the Department’s Student Services Officer serves as the student’s primary contact regarding department and university procedures and can provide information, assistance, and the appropriate forms and procedures for academic and financial matters. The SSO monitors academic progress and student completion of program requirements and milestones, which is reviewed as necessary by the DGS and discussed by faculty at an annual meeting devoted to assessing graduate student progress. Students who have made satisfactory academic progress are typically advanced to candidacy at the end of their second year in residency by faculty vote at this annual review meeting. Graduate Studies Committee The DGS, the track advisors (the DGS typically serves as track advisor for their track), and the SSO constitute the Graduate Studies Committee. All requests for funding that fall outside of allowed discretionary spending, extraordinary travel away from campus, petitions for leave of absence, and any disciplinary issues that may arise must be reviewed and, as necessary, approved by the Graduate Studies Committee. Expectations MA students are expected to meet regularly with their advisors and to keep them informed about their academic progress. To facilitate this, each student must meet with the DGS and the Track Advisor at the beginning of autumn quarter, again in winter quarter, and early in spring quarter during their first two years in the program. DGS and Track Advisors are available for these meetings at the beginning of each quarter. Additional Resources A detailed description of the program’s requirements, milestones, and advising expectations is found on the Classics website . Additionally, the program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE) and the Graduate Academic Policies (GAP). See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

Deadlines are October 13, 2026 for Winter, January 12, 2027 for Spring, and May 11, 2027 for Autumn 2027-28; decisions are expected about two weeks later.

Students in good standing receive a stipend, tuition and health insurance for the duration through mixed fellowship, dean and research-assistant funding, and are expected to seek internal and external awards.

Applicants need a bachelor's degree in engineering or physical science (or international equivalent), mathematics through multivariable calculus and linear algebra, unofficial transcripts, a 1-2 page personal statement, CV and recommendations. BMP is a full-time residential research PhD with first-year lab rotations, qualifying examination by the end of year two, and dissertation; the program describes a typical 5-6 years. Students making satisfactory academic progress receive tuition and living stipend throughout the doctorate. External fellowships are encouraged but not required.

Epidemiology and Clinical Research PhD applications and all recommendations are due December 1, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. through Stanford Graduate Admissions. Required materials are statement of purpose, three recommendations, unofficial transcripts, CV, and English test if not exempt. GRE is optional but encouraged; official transcripts are required only after an offer is accepted.

The Epidemiology department has limited MS and PhD funding, awarded at admission; prospective PhD students are encouraged to seek external and Stanford funding. Research or teaching assistantships may be discussed with individual professors after acceptance. Training grants support selected research areas, but PhD students need not join one.

The Epidemiology and Clinical Research MS is full-time and on campus, typically five to six quarters over two years. It requires 45 graduate units, a thesis normally based on original epidemiology research, overall B average, and B- or better in each core course.

Health Policy PhD students are guaranteed funding for the first five years; support can combine fellowships, grants, research assistantships and teaching assistantships. Admission capacity depends on available funding.

For Fall 2027 entry, the Human Genetics and Genetic Counseling MS deadline is December 1, 2026. Applicants must register with the Genetic Counseling Admissions Match before applying. facts.value: Biosciences PhD students complete at least two laboratory rotations; the recommended number and length vary by Home Program. Most coursework is completed in the first year, followed by research specialization and dissertation work.

MCP asks for a bachelor's or master's degree in any major, coursework in physiology, cell/developmental biology, basic biochemistry and molecular biology, and genetics, plus at least one university year each in physics, differential/integral calculus, and organic/inorganic chemistry. Research experience in biological sciences is especially valued.

Structural Biology PhD applicants need a bachelor's degree with at least one year of coursework in each of biology, mathematics, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, and physics. Original undergraduate research is particularly valued; GRE general and subject scores are not considered.

The 2026-27 Bulletin requires at least 46 program units and 135 university PhD units. Core epidemiology and biostatistics coursework precedes a written examination near the end of year two and an oral qualifying examination by Autumn of year three, then dissertation research. The Bulletin reports typical completion in four to four-and-a-half years.

For Autumn 2027-28 Health Policy PhD entry, the official application directory lists December 1, 2026 as the deadline and GRE General Test as required; no GRE Subject Test is considered. The program FAQ specifies no minimum GRE score and accepts scores up to three weeks after the deadline only when the test was taken before the deadline.

Health Policy PhD requires a U.S. bachelor's degree or international equivalent, online Stanford application with recommendations by the deadline, and a statement of purpose of at most two single-spaced pages identifying track and policy interests. No master's or minimum GPA is required. The program is full-time and in person; applying to the separate MS does not automatically follow from a PhD application.

Health Policy MS applicants should have clinical, healthcare, government or similar professional experience, though a medical degree is not required. The program is full-time and in person and offers no departmental fellowships or scholarships. U.S.-licensed physicians may substitute MCAT for GRE; exceptional GRE waivers require direct program approval.

The official coterm directory lists January 7, 2027 as the deadline for Autumn 2027-28 Community Health and Prevention Research MS entry, with two recommendations and a required program proposal. The program page limits coterm matriculation to Autumn and expects all materials by the deadline.

MCiM has no minimum GPA. Three recommendations are required; applicants who left full-time school within five years of June 2027 must include one recommendation from faculty at their last full-time school. Candidates whose last full-time study ended earlier need no faculty recommender.

The Human Genetics and Genetic Counseling MS is a two-year translational program combining coursework, research projects and clinical fieldwork rotations. It admits Fall entrants only; no formal part-time or fully remote route is offered.

value.A3i6E: Biochemistry is a department within the School of Medicine, with offices and labs in the Beckman Center for Molecular and Genetic Medicine at the Stanford Medical Center, the Shriram Center for Bioengineering and Chemical Engineering, and the Stanford Genome Technology Center. The Department of Biochemistry focuses on the molecular basis of life by studying the structures and functions of proteins and nucleic acids, the control of development, molecular motors and the cytoskeleton, trafficking of proteins between organelles, regulation of gene expression, protein homeostasis, structure and design, genetic and epigenetic control of chromosome function, and the application of genomics, all toward the understanding of health and disease.
value.ItCSB: The program of study is designed to prepare students for productive careers in biochemistry; its emphasis is training in research, and each student works closely with faculty members.
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Biochemistry is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Faculty advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, designing and conducting research, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

value.A3i6E: The Biomedical Data Science Program is interdepartmental and offers instruction and research opportunities leading to MS and PhD degrees in Biomedical Data Science. All students must complete the core curriculum requirements and additional coursework that fulfills degree requirements and pursues their technical interests and goals as specified for each degree program. The program can provide flexibility and complement Stanford’s other applied medical research opportunities. Special arrangements may be made for those with unique needs or those simultaneously enrolled in other degree programs within the university. Similarly, students with prior relevant training may have the curriculum adjusted to eliminate requirements met as part of prior training. The GRE is not required for admission. See Graduate Degrees for university requirements for the MS degree. Advising Upon entering the program, each student is assigned an academic advisor to help with course selection and monitor progress toward program milestones and degree requirements. Each research-track (academic) MS and PhD student conducts research under the primary mentorship of a faculty supervisor, who guides their scholarly and professional development. Further details about the advisor roles and responsibilities are found in DBDS Student Handbook . Master of Science in Biomedical Data Science (Academic) This degree is designed for individuals who wish to undertake an in-depth study of biomedical data science with research on a full-time basis. Typically, a student spends two years in the program and implements and documents a substantial project by the end of the second year. The first year involves acquiring the fundamental concepts and tools through coursework and research project involvement. Academic MS students are expected to devote 50 percent or more of their time to participating in research projects. Research rotations are not required but can be done with the approval of the academic advisor or training program director. Graduates of this program are prepared to contribute creatively to basic or applied projects in biomedical data science. This degree requires a written research paper to be approved by two faculty members. Master of Science in Biomedical Data Science (Professional/Honors Cooperative Program) This degree is designed primarily for the working professional with advanced training in one discipline who wishes to acquire interdisciplinary skills. Although many classes necessary for the degree are available online, some requirements may be fulfilled by implementing an alternative plan to be approved by the program. The professional MS is offered with the Stanford Engineering Center for Global & Online Education (CGOE), which establishes tuition and fee rates. The program uses the honors cooperative program (HCP) model, which assumes that the student works full time and is enrolled in the MS part-time. Students who live locally may attend their courses on campus. Students have up to five years to complete the program. Research projects are optional; the student must make arrangements with program faculty if interested. Graduates of this program are prepared to contribute creatively to basic or applied projects in biomedical data science. Master of Science in Biomedical Data Science (Coterminal) The coterminal degree program allows Stanford University undergraduates to study for a master’s degree while completing their bachelor’s degree(s) in the same or a different department. See Coterminal Master's Degrees for additional information. The coterminal Master of Science program follows the same program requirements as the Master of Science (Professional), except for the requirement to be employed full-time. The coterminal degree is available only to current Stanford undergraduates. Coterminal students are enrolled full time, and courses are taken on campus. Research projects are optional; the student must make arrangements with program faculty if interested. Graduates of this program are prepared to contribute creatively to basic or applied projects in biomedical data science.
value.WOZxr: Per Stanford Graduate Academic Policy , all courses for the Biomedical Data Science MS must be completed at Stanford.
value.ItCSB: The program in Biomedical Data Science emphasizes research to develop novel computational methods that can advance biomedicine. Students receive training in investigating new approaches to conceptual modeling and developing new algorithms that address challenging problems in the biological sciences and clinical medicine. Students primarily interested in developing new informatics methods and knowledge are best suited for this program. Students with a primary interest in the biological or medical application of existing informatics techniques may be better suited for training in the application areas.
value.advisingExpectations: The Program in Biomedical Data Science is committed to providing academic and research advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. When most effective, this advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by both the advisor and the advisee. As a best practice, advising expectations should be periodically discussed and reviewed to ensure mutual understanding. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship, proactively seeking academic and professional guidance and taking responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. The program’s student services staff is also essential to the student advising team. They inform students and advisors about university and department requirements, procedures, and opportunities and maintain the official records of advising assignments and approvals. Academic Adviser —Each new student in the Program in Biomedical Data Science is assigned an academic advisor (a member of the core or advising faculty or Executive Committee of the program). Academic advisors guide students in critical areas such as selecting courses, discussing research rotations, developing teaching pedagogy, navigating policies and degree requirements, and exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways. Usually, the academic advisor serves for the duration of the student’s study; the DBDS Student Handbook describes a process for formal advisor changes. In addition, the program director is available during the academic year by email and during office hours. The program director and student services staff monitor academic progress and student completion of program requirements and milestones. They are discussed by faculty during periodic meetings devoted to assessing graduate student progress. A detailed description of the program’s requirements, milestones, and advising expectations are listed in the Biomedical Data Science Training Program Student Handbook, on the program website , and in the section on the Biomedical Data Science Program. Research Adviser —Each student in the academic MS degree program must also have a research advisor chosen by mutual agreement at the end of their research rotations (typically by the end of their first year in the program). This research advisor is a core or advising faculty member for the DBDS program. The research advisor may not be the same person as the academic advisor. Research advisors and the students should have a clear, shared understanding of the scientific objectives of the student’s work and how it fits into a research program that will lead to an MS degree. They should focus on developing novel, generally applicable, and well-grounded methods in the informatics literature. In select cases, the research advisor may be a member of the collaborating faculty, in which case the student must have a co-adviser from the DBDS core or advising faculty. When there is a secondary or co-adviser, the primary advisor and co-adviser should clearly understand their mentorship roles. Additionally, the program adheres to the university policies, guidelines, and responsibilities that apply to all faculty-student advising relationships. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.
value.cotermTransferPolicy: In this master’s program, courses taken during or after the first quarter of the sophomore year are eligible for consideration for transfer to the graduate career; the timing of the first graduate quarter is not a factor. No courses taken prior to the first quarter of the sophomore year may be used to meet master’s degree requirements.
value.programGPARequirement: An overall GPA of 3.0 or higher is required for graduation.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Core Courses (12 units for Academic + Co-term MS; 9 units for Honors Coop)
published_requirement_narratives.text: Core courses must all be taken for a letter grade. All core courses are required for HCP except BMDS 212, which is highly recommended if possible. BMDS 212 requires special arrangements with the instructor, so we can include you in the class remotely if possible. Students are expected to participate regularly in the Biomedical Data Science Student Seminar and a research colloquium which is listed as BMDS 201A, B and C in fall/winter/spring quarters. Regardless of their enrollment, they should attend all meetings throughout their graduate training and a research colloquium appropriate to their interests. This course can be taken up to three times for one unit credit each time.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: CS/Stats/Math/Eng Electives
published_requirement_narratives.text: CS 106A and 106B do not count toward this Electives category. Crosslisted offerings for any of the courses listed above are accepted in place of the offering listed.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Computer Science, Statistics, Mathematics & Engineering (18 Units)
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students are expected to create a program of study with graduate-level courses in computer science, statistics, and other technical informatics-related disciplines to achieve in-depth mastery. The program of study may focus on aspects of these disciplines, including machine learning, statistical modeling, artificial intelligence, data mining, image analysis, human-computer interaction, and data visualization. Please note: Up to eight CS/Stats/Math/Eng units can be taken pass/fail. No more than nine units can be courses below the 200-level. course Programming Methodology and course Programming Abstractions cannot be counted for this requirement.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Social and Ethical Issues (4 units)
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students are expected to be familiar with issues regarding responsible conduct of research, reproducibility of research, and ethical, legal, social, organizational, and behavioral aspects of the impact of biomedical data science technologies on society. Note: MED 255 is required only for Academic MS and PhD students. These courses may be taken on a Satisfactory/No credit basis.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Unrestricted Electives
published_requirement_narratives.text: Unrestricted Units: 11 units for Academic + Coterm MS students; 14 units for Honors Coop. These can be any graduate-level courses at Stanford at or above the 100 level (subject to degree-specific limits).

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Academic MS Research Requirement
published_requirement_narratives.text: All students in the Academic MS program must engage in biomedical data-science-related research under the supervision of a Faculty member. Labs are arranged by mutual agreement between the student and the research supervisor. Before graduating from the Academic MS program, students must write a research paper reviewed and approved by two faculty members, including the Research Advisor.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Master's Requirements (45 units of coursework required to graduate; scroll down for HCP and Coterminal info)
published_requirement_narratives.text: Additional Requirements and Information: Completing the Department of Biomedical Data Science (DBDS) MS program with an overall GPA of 3.0 or higher is required for graduation. No one is required to take courses in an area in which they have already been adequately trained; under such circumstances, students are permitted to skip those courses and substitute more advanced work using a formal annual waiver process administered by the DBDS executive committee. At least 24 units of formal letter-graded coursework are expected for all MS and PhD candidates. Unrestricted Electives needed to complete 45 units. Students may fulfill this requirement with any Stanford graduate courses, including courses taken to satisfy program prerequisites. At least 23 units of courses must be at level 200 or above. Students are expected to participate regularly in BMDS 201 Biomedical Data Science Student Seminar and a research colloquium. An Academic MS student funded by the program must be a teaching assistant for one course; those students may register for 1-3 BMDS 295 Biomedical Informatics Teaching Methods units. HCP professional master’s students who are local are encouraged to participate in on-campus coursework and seminars. Masters students should sign up for BMDS 801 TGR Master’s Project for their project units after completing their 45-unit residency requirement. Students design appropriate programs for their interests with the assistance and approval of their Biomedical Data Science academic advisor.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Core Courses
published_requirement_narratives.text: Nine units for HCP students. (See Core Courses above for a list of required classes) Although many classes necessary for the degree are available online, some requirements may be fulfilled by implementing an alternative plan to be approved by the program. BIOMEDIN 212 requires special arrangements with the instructor, so we can include you in the class remotely if possible. Note that core courses should be taken for a grade, not pass/no credit

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Computer Science, Statistics, Mathematics &  Engineering (HCP Specific)
published_requirement_narratives.text: Complete at least 18 units of Computer science, statistics, mathematics, and engineering electives. Courses that can count for CS/Stats/Math/Eng are listed above. Up to eight CS/Stats/Math/Eng units can be taken pass/fail. CS 161 and STATS 200 are required, along with either STATS 315A or CS 229. These three courses, or some of their prerequisites, may not be available through SCPD. You should submit a course plan with the next best alternatives: these may include similar courses at Stanford or other institutions (note that outside courses would not count towards the required 45 units).

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Computer Science, Statistics, Mathematics &  Engineering (HCP Specific)
published_requirement_narratives.text: HCP Variation If Stats 200 is not offered remotely, then you can consider taking: MS&E 226 or EPI 259 and EPI 261 (both).

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Social & Ethical Issues (HCP Specific)
published_requirement_narratives.text: See the complete list of courses above in Social & Ethical Issues. Note that although MED 255 is listed as required, it is required only for MS and PhD students engaged in NIH-funded research at Stanford. This typically does not apply to HCP students.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Honors Cooperative Program
published_requirement_narratives.text: Additional Requirements and Information How to put the courses in order. Use one of the course flowsheets . First, check ExploreCourses and the SCPD website for which quarter the courses are offered. Also, check the listed prerequisites for each class and also the course websites for additional information about what’s expected so you can estimate how difficult each class will be for you. Typically, SCPD students take one course per quarter. Note that SCPD imposes an upper limit of three courses per quarter. Also, use the DBDS Student Wiki for advice on courses. 45 units are required for the MS. All courses counted towards the MS must be at or above the 100 level. You can include up to 18 units that you took Non-Degree Option before entering the MS program. At least 23 units must be courses at or above the 200 level. At least 24 units must be taken for a grade.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Coterminal Master's Additional Information
published_requirement_narratives.text: The coterminal degree program allows Stanford university undergraduates to study for a master’s degree while completing their bachelor’s degree(s) in the same or a different department. See Coterminal Master's Degree section for additional information. The coterminal Master of Science program follows the same program requirements as the Honors Cooperative, except for the requirement to be employed full-time. The coterminal degree is available only to current Stanford undergraduates. Coterminal students are enrolled full time and courses are taken on campus. Research projects are optional; the student must make arrangements with program faculty if interested. Graduates of this program are prepared to contribute creatively to basic or applied projects in biomedical data science. Application to the Coterminal Program For complete information, see the program’s Coterminal Master's Degree page. Submit the university Coterminal Online Application . Submit your academic resume or curriculum vitae. Submit a one-page Statement of Purpose describing how and why the DBDS program is well matched to your interests. University Coterminal Requirements Coterminal master’s degree candidates are expected to complete all master’s degree requirements as described in the Degrees section. Graduate Degrees lists university requirements for the master’s degree. After accepting admission to this coterminal master’s degree program, students may request a transfer of courses from the undergraduate to the graduate career to satisfy the requirements for the master’s degree. Transferring courses to the graduate career requires review and approval of both the undergraduate and graduate programs on a case-by-case basis. In this master’s program, courses taken three quarters before the first graduate quarter or later are eligible for consideration for transfer to the graduate career. No courses taken before the first quarter of the sophomore year may be used to meet master’s degree requirements. Course transfers are not possible after the bachelor’s degree has been conferred. The university requires that the graduate advisor be assigned in the student’s first graduate quarter even though the undergraduate career may still be open. The university also requires that the Master’s Degree Program Proposal be completed by the student and approved by the department by the end of the student’s first graduate quarter. DBDS Coterminal Requirements You are required to have at least 180 units (undergraduate) and 45 units (graduate). No units may be counted toward both undergraduate and DBDS MS degrees. 45 units are required for the MS. All courses counted towards the MS must be DBDS -related courses at or above the 100 level (as approved by the advisor and DBDS program). At least 23 units must be courses at or above the 200 level. At least 24 units must be taken for a grade. DBDS core courses may not be taken pass/fail. Exceptions: BMDS 201, BMDS 205, BMDS 295, BMDS 801, and MED 255, or BMDS courses that are offered only on an S/NC basis . A complete list of elective courses that can count for CS/Stats/Math/Eng is listed above. Up to eight CS/Stats/Math/Eng units can be taken pass/fail. You can apply to DBDS upon completion of 120 units but no later than the quarter before the expected completion of the undergraduate degree. Coterminal students are permitted to count coursework taken in the three quarters immediately before their first graduate quarter toward their graduate degree (summer quarter is not included in the count). The Coterminal Course Transfer eForm is used to transfer courses from the undergraduate to the graduate career and vice versa. This must be done before the undergraduate degree is conferred. You may take any course you want at Stanford while in the program, including electives not at all related to DBDS , as long as you also have an approved DBDS -related 45-unit program of study that satisfies the requirements for the DBDS degree.

value.A3i6E: The Master of Science in Clinical Informatics Management program (MCiM) is an intensive, one-year professional master’s degree combining business and technology constructs directed toward our migration to value in health care. MCiM is housed within the Clinical Excellence Research Center in the School of Medicine. The program offers students a unique experience of both remote and weekend onsite sessions to fit the needs of working professionals. Master of Science in Clinical Informatics Management courses provide rich learning experiences for students through a collaborative environment and dynamic course content. Through the coursework, students gain a deep understanding of health informatics and the business insights to accurately leverage technology to succeed in the real world. COVID-19 has reinforced the longstanding need for leaders who can expertly navigate business, technology, and medicine to manage and drive the digital transformation of a $4.0 trillion health care system. Diverse applications such as telemedicine for routine clinical care and digital radiology for the rapid diagnosis of COVID pneumonia are among some of the opportunities the crisis has highlighted. Others include greater capabilities for remote health monitoring, wearable sensors for monitoring patients, the health of populations on college campuses and in the workforce, and interactive voice-response tools such as Alexa, Siri, or Hey Google to provide new patient care services. Behind the scenes, machine learning has been rapidly adopted in applications as diverse as screening potential therapies for application to COVID and profiling symptoms that might indicate infection. Failures of the existing health care infrastructure have also been glaringly illustrated by the lack of interoperable data between hospitals and between the public and private sectors, as well as the lack of access to real-time data and reports as the COVID situation rapidly unfolded. Together, these scenarios call for leadership that brings together technology and clinical business units in entirely new ways. MCiM develops managers and senior leaders who have a keen understanding of the strategic business concepts and data science principles fundamental to raising the quality and efficiency of care delivery, in the COVID era and beyond. The founder of MCiM, Kevin Schulman, Professor of Medicine (Hospital Medicine) and, by courtesy, of Operations, Information and Technology at the Graduate School of Business, built the country’s first clinical informatics management program at Duke University in 2011. Graduates from that program have moved into management and senior leadership roles such as CEO, CIO, CMIO, CHIO, and Health Care IT Director.
value.WOZxr: The Master of Science in Clinical Informatics Management (MCiM) program does not allow students to transfer in credits. The MCiM program maintains a set curriculum for graduate students. MCiM students are required to enroll in the required courses set by the program. Prior to each quarter's enrollment period, MCiM students will receive enrollment instructions with details of the courses required for minimum degree progress.
value.ItCSB: Develop and apply business models, clinical informatics tools, and ethics insights to a variety of scenarios and settings in organizations ranging from health care-focused technology start-ups to large, established health systems. Acquire the knowledge and tools to successfully design, implement, and manage digital innovations to improve the cost-effectiveness and the quality of patient care. Deploy new management skills to lead multidisciplinary teams in data analytics and data science, medicine, and business in your own organization and across institutions.
value.advisingExpectations: Students in the program will be assigned a program advisor, and will be expected to meet with them on a quarterly basis.
value.programGradingPolicies: MCiM students must enroll in the required courses for a letter grade, and must enroll for the number of units detailed in the instructions.
value.programAdditionalPolicies: Attendance Policy MCiM is a one-year, full-time program designed to be completed across four quarters, with onsite class weekends held generally every other Friday and Saturday. Attendance is central to the learning model. An "onsite session" refers to one day of an onsite class weekend. All missed sessions count toward a student's quarterly absence limit, including absences due to illness. Students are not able to join onsite classes remotely, and classes are not recorded for absent students. Students must submit the MCiM Attendance Form at least one hour before the start of an on-campus class day to receive credit for advance notice. Advance notice should also be reported directly to instructors, except in emergencies. If the form is not submitted, the absence is treated as without advance notice. Per quarter, the following limits apply: With advance notice: 3 absences: warning 4 absences: academic probation and a required meeting with the MCiM Director of Graduate Studies 5 or more absences: dismissal from the program Without advance notice: 2 absences: warning 3 absences: academic probation and a required meeting with the MCiM Director of Graduate Studies 4 or more absences: dismissal from the program Students who anticipate difficulty maintaining good standing under this policy should contact the MCiM Admin Team before the start of the onsite weekend to discuss options.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Course Requirements
published_requirement_narratives.text: CIM 202 will be taken over the course of four consecutive quarters, for a total of four units. CIM 200 will be taken over the course of three consecutive quarters, for a total of six units. CIM 215 must be taken over the course of two consecutive quarters, for a total of two units.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Course Requirements
published_requirement_narratives.text: Students take a set of required courses during each of the four academic quarters. These courses reflect the overall set curriculum of the program and cannot be taken at alternative quarters. The required curriculum consists of six business courses, six information technology courses, an ethics course, and a practicum course. Currently, there are no elective courses offered through the program. The complete schedule of courses is listed. All courses are required. No substitutions are permitted. To complete the Master's in Clinical Informatics Management, students must complete a minimum of 48 units. During quarters two, three, and four, students complete a practicum course, with the bulk of the effort for this course occurring in quarter four. MCiM courses must be taken for a letter grade.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: MCiM Program Proposal
published_requirement_narratives.text: MCiM students are required to submit a program proposal at least two weeks before the final study list due date of their first quarter of enrollment. Due to MCiM’s set curriculum, a pre-filled proposal is available for MCiM students on the MCiM Resource Hub. Students must sign and submit the proposal to the MCiM administration; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal from the program. As there are no shifts in curriculum or electives allowed, there should be no need to revise the program proposal after submission.
