value.description: The PhD degree requires coursework and independent research demonstrating an individual’s creative, scholastic, and intellectual abilities. On entering the department, students are oriented to the curriculum and the timetable for completing the degree requirements by the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) and the Student Services Officer (SSO).
value.interpretation_boundary: Published study content and degree structure; this overview does not replace the selected route admission requirements.

value.description: Learn how to approach and solve research problems by developing skills in modern methods of neuroscience research, the ability to appraise the scientific literature and make scientific judgments, and ultimately, to function as an independent creative neuroscientist.
value.interpretation_boundary: Published study content and degree structure; this overview does not replace the selected route admission requirements.

value.description: The graduate program in Structural Biology is intended to prepare students for careers as independent investigators in cell and molecular biology. The principal requirement of a PhD degree is the completion of research constituting an original and significant contribution to advancing knowledge. It is training in a major with connections to biophysics (e.g., physics, chemistry, or biology, with a quantitative background equivalent to that of an undergraduate physics or chemistry major at Stanford). Current research topics in the department lie in gene expression; theoretical, crystallographic, and genetic analysis of protein structure; and cell-cell interaction. See Stanford’s School of Medicine website for further information. Admission Applicants to the program should have a bachelor’s degree and complete at least a year of coursework in biology, mathematics, organic chemistry, physical chemistry, and physics. The department must receive applications before December 15 for notification by April 15. Application to the National Science Foundation for fellowship support is also encouraged. Prospective applicants should contact the Department of Structural Biology for further information. The GRE general score is optional, and the GRE subject score is not required. It is recommended that prospective applicants have completed the following courses (or their equivalent) before applying: UNITS course Organic Polyfunctional Compounds 3 course Foundations of Physical Chemistry 4 course Physical Chemistry II 3 course Physical Chemistry III 3 course Applied Biochemistry 2
value.interpretation_boundary: Published study content and degree structure; this overview does not replace the selected route admission requirements.

conditions: The Bulletin overview includes a December 15 deadline and optional GRE General wording. The current departmental 2027 application page specifies December 1, 2026 at 11:59:59 p.m. PST and does not consider GRE General or Subject. Preserve the source wording as reference, but use the separately scoped current application records for applying.

value.description: The Stanford Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine (SCBRM) program is dedicated to doctoral education that translates basic science to clinical applications, typically called Translational Science, and is of intense interest internationally in medical schools and universities. Our doctoral program provides exceptional didactic education and research experience in the basic sciences underlying stem cell biology. In addition, program participants will receive specialized training in developing and clinically applying discoveries in the basic sciences to achieve regenerative therapies. Thus, our graduates will be uniquely positioned to develop successful translational careers in Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine. They will emerge prepared to deliver on their passion for improving the human condition. The core curriculum combines unique research and clinical/professional immersion rotations to provide opportunities for doctoral students to specialize in the broad subject of translational medicine and yet focus specifically on the fundamentals of SCBRM. The curriculum combines genetics and developmental biology education with an introductory laboratory-based stem cell course, an advanced course in stem cell biology and regenerative medicine, and a clinical rotation with alternative law, business, and/or engineering opportunities.
value.interpretation_boundary: Published study content and degree structure; this overview does not replace the selected route admission requirements.

facts.value: MBA applicants require U.S. bachelor degree or equivalent (including eligible international three-year degrees); no minimum GPA. All applicants submit GMAT or GRE (no minimum, no superscore, only one test sitting reported); Executive Assessment not accepted. For 2026-27, scores expiring before Jun 1, 2027 should be officially reported at application submission and may arrive after deadline. English test (TOEFL, IELTS Academic or PTE Academic) is required if undergraduate classes were not all taught exclusively in English, unless later graduate program was exclusively English; citizenship/work experience do not exempt. Minimums: TOEFL 100 before Jan 21 2026 or 5.0 on/after, IELTS 7.0, PTE 68; scores valid two years and test must precede round deadline. Application includes education/transcripts, personal/activities/awards, professional experience and resume, two recommendations (preferably supervisors), essays, optional short answer, fee. Unofficial transcripts at application, official after admission. Application decisions are holistic; calculus/statistics/microeconomics strengthen readiness but are not formal prerequisites.
conditions: English test exemption depends on all courses in undergraduate or later graduate study having been exclusively English.
English scores expire after two years and must be valid on round deadline.
GMAT/GRE scores must be submitted from one sitting and are not superscored.
exceptions: A joint MBA/MSx application requires valid GMAT, GMAT Focus, or GRE because EA is not accepted for MBA.

facts.value: For Fall 2027 entry, completed application including recommendations and fee is due by 4:00 p.m. Pacific Time: Round 1 2026-09-09; Round 2 2027-01-06; Round 3 2027-04-07. Decision notifications are 2026-12-09, 2027-04-01, and 2027-05-27 respectively. Applicants may apply once per application year in one round.
conditions: Late material may not be reviewed.
Admitted students are expected to enroll in the admission year; deferral is limited to rare and extraordinary circumstances.
exceptions: Applicants applying to MBA and MSx together must use Round 2.

facts.value: First-year MBA 2026-27 estimated cost of attendance is USD 140,940 for a single student and USD 168,825 for a married student; tuition is USD 89,187 per year in this annual budget. Living expenses, housing, medical insurance and health fee are separately estimated; global-experience costs of USD 4,000-6,000 are excluded. Financial aid is a separate assessment; budget adjustments can increase loan eligibility and do not typically increase fellowship awards.
conditions: Amounts are first-year annual estimates and vary by household, insurance, and allowable budget adjustments.

facts.value: MSx is a 12-month full-time in-person Stanford GSB MS in Management. Applicants require a U.S. bachelor’s degree or equivalent (international three-year degrees included); only rare exceptions are considered. At least eight years of post-graduate professional work experience is required; managerial experience is valued but not required. No minimum GPA; application requires education history/transcripts, test score, professional history/resume (maximum two pages), two recommendations, essays and fee. GMAT, GRE or Executive Assessment is required before application with no test waivers; LSAT/MCAT are not substitutes. TOEFL/PTE/IELTS is required if English was not the primary language of instruction or any classes used another language; online PTE not accepted. Applicants report only one testing session if repeated; online GMAT/GRE/EA/TOEFL/IELTS accepted. 2026-27 rounds: Oct 8 2026, Jan 6 2027 (MBA/MSx joint), and Feb 11 2027, all 4 p.m. Pacific; decisions Dec 9 2026 or Apr 1 2027. Nonrefundable fee USD 275. A 12-month 2026-27 cost estimate is USD 221,190 single / USD 258,342 married, including tuition USD 154,828. Need-based fellowships and loans are available to admitted students regardless of citizenship; admissions decisions precede aid application.
conditions: MSx has no test waivers. Valid test score is required to receive an interview invitation.
English test is required under either language-of-instruction condition; no general nationality-based exemption is stated in the reviewed page.
Cost is for the 12-month period July 2026 to June 2027 and includes insurance even if alternative coverage exists.
exceptions: Joint applicants need GMAT or GRE because the MBA does not accept EA.
Applicants may apply once per application year. Deferral is considered only in rare extraordinary circumstances.
Need-based funding is decided only for admitted students and is available regardless of citizenship.

facts.value: GSB PhD applicants must hold, or expect before enrollment, a U.S. bachelor's degree or recognized international equivalent. A complete application includes a statement of purpose, CV, three references, GRE, TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic if applicable, uploaded official transcripts, online submission, and a USD 125 application fee. No minimum GPA, GRE score, particular prior field, work experience, or MBA/graduate degree is required. Applicants may also apply to another Stanford program. All applicants must submit GRE scores, including every administration from Dec 1, 2021 through Dec 1, 2026 for Fall 2027; GRE At Home is accepted. Self-reported and official GRE scores are required, but self-reported scores suffice for initial review while official results are pending; do not superscore. Official GRE scores go to ETS code 4704. Applicants without an English-test exemption must submit TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic; minimums are TOEFL 100 for tests before Jan 21, 2026, TOEFL 5 for tests on/after that date, or IELTS 7. For Autumn 2027, English test dates must fall from Dec 1, 2024 through Dec 1, 2026. TOEFL MyBest scores are accepted; IELTS superscores are not. Official English scores are required, with self-reporting sufficient for initial review while official scores are pending.
conditions: International degree equivalence may be checked with WES; this is a recommendation, not a Stanford credential evaluation.
Field choice determines research area and related preparation.
English-test exemption may require supporting documentation as a condition of admission.
Admitted students accepting an offer must take the Stanford English Placement Test if their application TOEFL was below 109 or IELTS below 8.
exceptions: English scores are not required at application if the applicant is a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, has English as a first language, earned a U.S. bachelor, master, or doctoral degree (or international equivalent) at a university where all instruction was in English, or has at least two consecutive years of professional or educational experience in English within the past 10 years.

facts.value: GSB PhD is one Business Administration PhD award with seven fields of study: Accounting; Economic Analysis & Policy; Finance; Marketing; Operations, Information & Technology; Organizational Behavior; and Political Economics. The program is five to six years full time in Stanford, California. Incoming doctoral students receive a financial fellowship covering tuition, living stipend, and health fees for five years, conditional on satisfactory academic progress and program milestones, with a possible sixth-year extension. Incoming students in 2026-27 receive a living stipend of USD 59,500 annually. Research and course assistantships are typically included in the support package; professional development grants cover eligible conference travel, publication submissions, and professional organization fees.
conditions: The USD 59,500 stipend is an annual 2026-27 incoming-student amount, not a Fall 2027 award quote.
Five-year support depends on satisfactory academic progress and program milestones; a sixth year is possible rather than automatic.
The reviewed financial-aid page does not specify a separate summer stipend amount or payment schedule.

facts.value: For Fall 2027, a bachelor degree or equivalent must be completed or expected by Summer 2027; all offers are conditional on graduation. LSAC application opens Sep 15, 2026 and is due Feb 15, 2027 11:59 p.m. PT; KHS files must be complete Dec 1, 2026. Required: 1-2 page resume, roughly two-page personal statement, required viewpoint essay (1-2 pages), 250-word answer to one of three prompts, 2-4 LSAC letters, CAS transcript report, LSAT or GRE. Valid LSAT scores must all be reported; score dates before June 2021 invalid, Argumentative Writing required, latest LSAT Jan 2027. GRE-only route permitted; GRE scores before June 2021 invalid, all valid scores submitted, suggested test by Feb 1 2027. Fee USD 85; SLS fee waiver must be requested before application, with 5-7 business days processing. No admissions interviews. Rolling decisions (accept/reject/waitlist), first response target Apr 30. Deposit secures enrollment; limited one-year deferral requires nonrefundable tuition deposit; waitlist admits cannot defer. SLS may withdraw offers for significant performance decline, misrepresentation, serious integrity concerns, or another law-school enrollment commitment/deposit.
conditions: All application items are applicant responsibility; file is complete only when required records arrive.
Fee waiver request must precede LSAC submission; current fee-waiver instruction page gives 5-7 business day processing.
exceptions: If an applicant has any valid LSAT, it must be reported; GRE-only applicants may omit LSAT.
Admissions Committee does not interview applicants.
Waitlist admits cannot defer.

facts.value: Four LLM specializations: Corporate Governance & Practice, Environmental Law & Policy, International Economic Law, Business and Policy, and Law, Science & Technology; primary law degree must be earned outside U.S. SPILS is a research-oriented route for foreign-law-degree holders; the JSM is awarded through SPILS and requires JD/equivalent plus participation. LLM and SPILS have separate admissions decisions. JSD applicants have two routes: Stanford SPILS graduates and students from Stanford/other U.S. law schools who complete an LLM before JSD; LLM-route applicants submit serious independent original research. Neither SPILS nor Stanford LLM admission guarantees JSD. MLS is a nonprofessional degree for a small number of advanced graduate students/scholars without legal training; Bulletin inventory confirms it is not coterm.
conditions: LLM and SPILS admit small cohorts; MLS admits very few if any.
JSD antecedent route must be complete before starting the JSD; application is a separate selection decision.
exceptions: Current JSD program page resolves the initial ambiguity: U.S.-based law-school LLM applicants are also a stated route, alongside SPILS completers.
MLS is not a coterm degree.

facts.value: LLM/SPILS Fall 2027 applications open Sep 15, 2026 and are due Dec 1, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. PT; KHS file-complete deadline is same date. JSD application opens Feb 2027 and deadline is Apr 2027, both officially TBA. Advanced app fee USD 85 per program; separate fee for each program. Shared LSAC application materials: 1-2 page resume, 2-3 page personal statement, two recommendation letters, official transcripts, TOEFL; SPILS/JSD add research proposal and third letter; JSD also requires 1-2 examples of English scholarly writing. LSAC CAS and recommendation service required; direct submissions rejected. TOEFL iBT minimum is 100 before Jan 21, 2026; for tests on/after that date, overall 5.5 with reading/listening at least 5.5 and writing/speaking at least 5.0. Scores to LSAC institution code 8395. Native-English applicants still request TOEFL waiver; full-time study/work in English for at least two years may qualify with formal request/evidence. LLM normally expects two years legal practice; waiver explanation possible. Decisions expected by mid-April 2027.
conditions: All required documents must arrive through LSAC services.
Applicants under two years legal practice need an unusual-circumstances waiver explanation for LLM.
English proficiency required; eligible waiver must be formally requested with proof.
exceptions: JSD application dates are TBA, and its KHS application must be submitted in a prior masters-application year.

facts.value: 2026-27 JD standard cost-of-attendance estimate is USD 125,124 on-campus or USD 126,216 off-campus for a single student; tuition is USD 79,779. Need-based aid uses FAFSA and CSS Profile and combines tuition fellowships, government/private loans; it is re-evaluated annually and level is not guaranteed for all three years. Stanford reports approximately 75-80% of students receive aid, with average fellowship portion USD 25,000-28,000 annually. Age-based parental contribution rules apply to CSS resource assessment. Yellow Ribbon is additional for eligible 100% Chapter 33 benefit recipients; LRAP is a post-JD loan assistance program for qualifying public-service employment.
conditions: Cost figures are standard single-student budget estimates; medical insurance is waivable and shown separately.
Need-based award depends on demonstrated need and annual review.
exceptions: Yellow Ribbon requires 100% Post-9/11 GI Bill eligibility; veteran benefits are not universal grants.
LRAP is post-graduation loan support, not tuition reduction at admission.

facts.value: For Fall 2027 MD admission, applicants need a recognized U.S. bachelor degree or equivalent; foreign bachelor degree holders may need WES equivalency and one in-person academic year at an accredited institution in the U.S., Canada, or U.K. Eligible groups include citizens, permanent residents, DACA, undocumented and visa-eligible international applicants; undocumented admits need legal status by matriculation. No required undergraduate courses; coursework areas are recommended. At least one MCAT after Jan 2023 and by Aug 22, 2026 is required. AMCAS due Oct 1, 2026 11:59 p.m. ET; invited applicants submit Stanford supplemental materials by Oct 9, 2026 11:59 p.m. PT. Three to six AMCAS letters, with at least three received by supplemental deadline; invitations to interview roll from August; decisions Jan-Mar; accept one offer by Apr 30. Fee is required but amount is not exposed; only AAMC Fee Assistance Program waiver approved before primary application is accepted. No Early Decision.
conditions: Timeline page does not identify its applicable entering class/cycle on the reviewed content; confirm before applying.
The 2026-entry how-to-apply page is historical and has not been used to set current MCAT dates.
exceptions: Supplemental application is by invitation after AMCAS receipt.

facts.value: Stanford MD Discovery Curriculum can be completed at different paces: pre-clerkship phase in two years or, after applying for the option, spread over three years. Students must pass USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK. 2026-27 regular MD tuition is USD 24,034 per quarter for Autumn, Winter, Spring, and Summer; research rate USD 3,993 per quarter applies under specified 100%-research/after-residency conditions. Insurance and mandatory fees may be additional.
conditions: Research tuition is conditional and not a general student rate.
Required tuition is quarter-based; annual total depends on enrollment status and additional fees.
exceptions: MD students enrolled in other Stanford degrees may be charged under separate rules.

facts.value: Current Stanford MD students may apply internally to MSTP, commonly after M1 or during M2/M2B, with later-stage cases discussed individually. They need good standing, a defined thesis and a committed adviser. Students outside Stanford MD and students enrolled in another institution's PhD are ineligible for this internal funding route. Current Stanford PhD students must be in good standing, have passed the qualifying exam, and apply to MD by fall of G3; MD admission is a separate decision. The published Autumn2026-27 funding deadline was January20,2026 at5p.m.Pacific and has passed. Materials include a cover page, statement of at most250words, mentor letter, access to the MD application, NIH biosketch, dual-degree form and research proposal. An oral presentation lasts10minutes followed by10minutes of questions. Funding start depends on availability, degree approvals and full-time thesis research.
conditions: The January20,2026 deadline does not establish the next internal funding cycle.
The internal admissions page restricts MSTP funding to US citizens and permanent residents.
exceptions: The internal application pathway is distinct from initial external MSTP/MD application.
Current Stanford PhD students have an eligibility path, but MD admission remains a separate decision.

facts.value: For the MSPA 2026-27 application timeline leading to August 2027 entry, CASPA opened Apr 30, 2026; the application had to be in Complete status in CASPA by Jul 15, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (deadline passed); interviews Autumn 2026 and orientation/classes begin Aug 2027. Only CASPA application status establishes deadline compliance; no other proof or evidence is accepted. Failure to maintain Complete status moving forward jeopardizes admission consideration. The only minimum admission requirement is a qualifying in-person U.S./Canada bachelor's degree or qualifying U.S. graduate degree by Jul 1 of the matriculation year (July 1, 2027 for August 2027 entry); no specific major. Foreign-degree-only applicants are ineligible, WES equivalency is not accepted, and no waiver applies. Recommended: GRE/MCAT/PA-CAT (PA-CAT preferred), preparatory coursework, 500+ clinical hours and three references. No minimum GPA or test score; one CASPA personal statement up to 5,000 characters. Three references recommended, max five; friends/family/healthcare providers excluded. About 10% interview. USD 1,000 nonrefundable seat deposit credited to first-quarter tuition; no advanced placement. Stanford undergraduate applicants may also apply as internal applicants through the same CASPA route; Stanford identifies no coterm degree or advanced placement for this program.
conditions: CASPA Complete status must be attained by the published deadline and maintained afterward; no other proof or evidence of completion is accepted, and processing extensions are not granted.
Test scores must be verified by the deadline to count; admitted applicants without PA-CAT may be required to complete it before enrollment, without affecting admission status.
exceptions: Tests, recommendations and preparatory coursework/experience are recommendations, not minimum admission conditions.
International applicants qualify only with the specified qualifying U.S./Canada degree; no degree waiver.
Internal Stanford undergraduate eligibility uses the same qualifying degree requirement and external CASPA application; no coterm route exists.

facts.value: For 2026-27 MSPA, standard tuition is USD 21,815 per quarter for nine quarters. Mandatory quarterly fees/books subtotal USD 850; disability insurance USD 40 annually. Cardinal Care is optional at USD 2,936 per quarter; private qualifying insurance may be used. Living estimates: USD 12,960 per quarter on campus, USD 14,435 off campus. Published total-program on-campus budget without Cardinal Care is USD 326,145 for AY 2026-27 matriculants, with future incremental tuition increases likely.
conditions: Standard progress assumes nine quarters; extra terms incur further charges.
Health insurance is mandatory but Cardinal Care is optional if qualifying private insurance is maintained.
exceptions: Housing and insurance choices change total attendance costs.

facts.value: MS in Medicine without subplan is reserved for MED-MD students. Berg Scholars Biomedical Investigation MS application is restricted to Stanford MD students approved for a split curriculum and at the end of the second year; approved off-cycle applications may be considered, but funding is not retroactive. Applicants should contact the program director early. Materials include a research proposal (maximum five pages), permission to access the AMCAS application, proposed mentor recommendation, brief career/coursework/committee/Gantt-chart statement, and oral presentation with Q&A. Application submission, review, interview, presentation and selection occur around the end of Summer Quarter after M2; decisions precede the next quarter. MS requires at least 45 unduplicated units (33 research and 12 coursework), completed within three years of the first graduate quarter while pursuing MD.
conditions: Applicants must be approved for split curriculum and be at end of M2.
Degree requirements must be completed within three years of first graduate quarter; MS and MD units cannot be duplicated toward residency.
exceptions: This is an internal additional award, not an open external MS admission route.
An approved off-cycle applicant may apply, but acceptance does not provide retroactive funding.

facts.value: The 12-month MSx program cost of attendance for July 2026-June 2027 is USD 221,190 for a single student and USD 258,342 for a married student; tuition is USD 154,828. Budget includes housing, living expenses, USD 250 documentation fee, medical insurance, health fee. Eligible child allowances are separately estimated. Need-based gap between attendance cost and expected student contribution is covered by a mix of fellowship and loans; fellowship is gift aid, based solely on demonstrated need, and is available regardless of citizenship.
conditions: Cost figures cover 12 months from July 2026 to June 2027; household costs differ.
Financial aid reviewed for admitted students after admission; need-based award is not an admission consideration.
exceptions: Applicants may receive fellowship and loan package regardless of citizenship.

facts.value: For Fall 2027 GSB PhD entry, the application portal sets the deadline at Dec 1, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time, including recommendation letters and other materials. Applications opened in early September 2026. Only applications complete by the deadline are guaranteed review. Admission decisions are typically available by mid-March and are sent by email. Admitted students are expected to enroll in September 2027; ordinarily they must reapply rather than defer.
conditions: The portal deadline applies to the GSB PhD application, not other Stanford graduate routes.
exceptions: GSB may consider deferral only for rare and extraordinary circumstances, such as compulsory military service.

facts.value: MD financial aid requires an application each academic year after admission offer; no application is reviewed before acceptance. U.S. citizens/permanent residents are considered for need-based Stanford grants and loans and federal loans; international students cannot receive Direct Loans but may apply for Stanford need-based grants/loans. All applicants complete CSS Profile, Stanford supplemental aid application and parent tax records; U.S. citizens/permanent residents also complete FAFSA. Parent finances are generally considered regardless of age; absolute estrangement waiver requires third-party evidence. Institutional aid is need-based, not merit-based. Outside scholarships, MedScholars and RA/TA have separate applications. MSTP and KHS students typically do not apply for regular aid.
conditions: Aid application is annual; required parent information and tax documents apply with limited documented exceptions.
exceptions: International students are ineligible for Direct Loans but can be considered for Stanford institutional need-based aid.

facts.value: External MSTP uses the same AMCAS, Stanford supplemental application and policies as MD. Applicants are first reviewed for MSTP; applicants not selected for MSTP interview are routed to MD Admissions. MSTP admission requires MD acceptance. Research experience is central, with three to six AMCAS letters and research mentor letters desired. Applicants matriculated in another institution MD or PhD program cannot apply; Stanford does not accept transfer applicants. All prospective students may apply, but MSTP stipend and tuition support are limited to U.S. citizens and permanent residents. International students may apply to MSTP only with Knight-Hennessy; otherwise MD and departmental PhD admissions are separate, and any PhD department funding is independently determined.
conditions: Combined degree admission is contingent on MD acceptance.
MSTP-funded places are citizenship-restricted.
exceptions: International applicants may pursue separate MD and department PhD paths; this is not MSTP-funded admission.

scope.cycle: 2025-26 Yellow Ribbon amount; aid eligibility page checked 2026-10-02

facts.value: U.S. citizens and permanent residents admitted to MSPA may be eligible for financial aid. Federal applicants meeting requirements are considered for Stafford and/or Grad PLUS loans; program funds are limited. NHSC and California underserved-area programs offer eligible loan repayment or scholarships. Yellow Ribbon contribution listed for MSPA is USD 13,500 in 2025-26 only. Financial aid is separate from admissions and full-time study strongly discourages employment.
conditions: Program support is limited; federal aid requires meeting Stanford deadlines/requirements.
exceptions: Yellow Ribbon figure is historical 2025-26, not confirmed for 2026-27.

facts.value: Stanford Law says it provides no scholarship or stipend funding to LLM students. SPILS funding exists only to an extremely limited degree. Admitted JSD students may receive some need-based aid and research/conference funding; no coverage amount or renewal terms are published. KHS is separately applied for; up to three years of funding may be available, with separate timing and eligibility. MLS program funding was not stated on reviewed official pages.
conditions: KHS requires separate application and does not automatically follow degree admission.
JSD support is described as some need-based aid and research/conference funds, with details unpublished.
exceptions: No SLS scholarship/stipend for LLM; extremely limited SPILS support; no amount identified.

facts.value: Stanford's official 2026-27 Law School tuition category is USD 26,593 per quarter; the published rate is by Law School classification and not limited to JD. LLM programs are nine months/three quarters, so the listed tuition rate establishes the applicable quarterly rate, while the standard single-student cost-of-attendance page separately estimates USD 125,124 on-campus or USD 126,216 off-campus. The COA page does not identify which advanced degree cases its living/loan budget covers. MLS requires at least three residency quarters and full Law School tuition; program-specific non-tuition fees or special registration changes should be confirmed.
conditions: USD 26,593 is per quarter and Law School classified; special registration or multiple-career tuition rules can change billing.
Standard COA totals are published school-wide but are not explicitly assigned to LLM/JSM/JSD/MLS budgets.
Non-tuition fees, insurance and household costs are separate from tuition.
exceptions: Do not report the standard single-student COA as a verified complete advanced-degree budget.
MLS residency requirement is at least three quarters; JSD students may enter TGR status under separate academic rules.

facts.value: All candidates must complete an interview before an offer. Interviews are invitation-only, behavioral and may be remote or in-person; an invitation is not an offer. A valid standardized test score must be on file before an interview invitation. Interview window: Round 1 mid-Sep-mid-Nov; Round 2 mid-Jan-mid-Mar; Round 3 mid-Apr-mid-May. Two to three candidates are generally interviewed per available seat. Admission is need-blind; admission decisions precede financial aid review.
conditions: Interview by invitation only and valid test score must be received; all admitted candidates are interviewed.
exceptions: Interview invitation does not guarantee admission.

facts.value: MBA aid is need-based and available to students of any citizenship who demonstrate need. After admission, students complete the Stanford GSB institutional application annually while enrolled. U.S. citizens/permanent residents submit FAFSA, institutional application, two prior years federal returns and most recent pay stub; international students submit institutional application and two years of tax statements from all countries of work. The gap between cost of attendance and expected contribution is covered by fellowships and loans; average class of 2026 fellowship was about USD 50,000/year or USD 100,000 total. Fellowships are need-based gifts. Financial aid application is separate and admissions is need-blind.
conditions: Need analysis expects student/spouse contribution; consumer debt is excluded.
Aid application and supporting tax materials are renewed annually.
exceptions: Need-based funding applies regardless of citizenship; federal loan eligibility differs by status.

facts.value: JD requires 111 units over no less than three academic years. LLM requires 35-45 approved quarter units, three quarters in residence, at least 26 Law units and full tuition; residence is at least 9 enrolled units and 8 passed units each quarter, with work limited to 20 hours weekly; LLM is a full nine-month academic year. JSM requires 35 units, with thesis and public presentation, and is expected to finish in one academic year (two consecutive years maximum). MLS requires 37 units, three residency quarters, and is expected to finish in one academic year (two consecutive years maximum). JSD requires 44 residency units, including one academic year in residence, and independent dissertation research; award duration beyond minimum residency is not specified.
conditions: These are academic completion requirements, not minimum duration guarantees except where stated.
Law residency requires full tuition and unit completion each quarter.
exceptions: JSD requires 44 residency units but only one academic year in residence under University minimum; actual completion time depends on dissertation/candidacy.

facts.value: Traditional Stanford MD is a four-year clinical degree. The Discovery Curriculum permits students to take pre-clerkship curriculum at full pace over two years or request to spread it over three years, which can extend the MD path to five years. Combined MD-PhD MSTP averages 7.5 years; students generally take six or eight years depending on research and commonly finish PhD requirements one or two years before final clinical rotations. The PA MS is nine quarters (captured separately).
conditions: MSTP completion length varies with individual research; MD pre-clerkship split option is an approved pathway.

facts.value: A qualifying bachelor degree must be completed by July 1 of the year of matriculation. Accepted: a bachelor from a regionally accredited US or Canadian institution (three-year Quebec; four-year other Canadian provinces), or a US graduate degree plus the equivalent undergraduate degree. Online bachelor programs, foreign-only degrees, WES substitution, and waivers are not accepted.

Current Stanford central loan policy says graduate students who have not borrowed for the current degree program before July 1, 2026 are not eligible for new Grad PLUS loans. The MSPA program page checked 2026-10-03 still lists Stafford and/or Grad PLUS; for new August 2027 entrants the two official pages conflict, so Grad PLUS availability must not be represented as generally available.

MD applicants may use AI for brainstorming, organizing their own ideas, identifying clarity issues, and light grammar/spelling edits preserving their voice. AI may not generate substantive responses or frameworks, substantially rewrite/paraphrase essays, or generate reflections, motivations, lessons or conclusions.

Stanford Law advanced applicants must submit TOEFL iBT (not IELTS under the current Law advanced process). Minimum: 100 for tests before Jan 21, 2026; for tests on/after, overall 5.5 with reading/listening >=5.5 and writing/speaking >=5.0. Native English does not automatically waive; applicants must request a waiver with evidence. Waivers may be granted for >=2 years full-time study or work in English. Law page does not specify a validity period; confirm with admissions if score age matters.
conditions: Law advanced-program English requirements are distinct from central nonprofessional thresholds; the common portal policy does not replace them.

facts.value: MSPA is a nine-quarter program with a summer break, clinical rotations, selected California clinical sites, leadership-track choice, and required thesis. Graduates are prepared for PANCE. value.A3i6E: The Earth Systems Program offers current Stanford University undergraduates the opportunity to apply for a one-year coterminal master’s program. The Earth Systems Program is interdisciplinary. Students may select the topic area where they’d like to advance their knowledge in consultation with their master’s advisor. Students learn about and investigate complex environmental problems caused by human activities in conjunction with natural changes in the Earth system. Earth Systems Coterm students gain advanced knowledge to tackle the world’s most pressing social-environmental problems and sustainability challenges.
value.WOZxr: Pre-requisite courses may be fulfilled through approved AP credit , Stanford placement tests , or transfer credit , where applicable. Students can submit a petition for such credit to be counted. Transfer courses from other institutions may not be counted toward the required 45 units.
value.ItCSB: The coterminal master’s degree in Earth Systems provides the student with enhanced analytical tools to evaluate the disciplines most closely associated with the student’s focus area. Specialization is gained through coursework and independent research work supervised by the master’s faculty advisor.
value.advisingExpectations: Purpose of Advising The primary purpose of the faculty advisor in the Earth Systems coterminal MS and MA programs is to help guide the academic development of their advisees. Faculty advisors help advisees design comprehensive, rigorous, interdisciplinary curricula that enable each student to acquire mastery of their chosen field(s). MS coterm students may choose to conduct research and write a master’s thesis under the guidance of their coterm advisor or another pre-approved advisor on academic council. Earth Systems staff members can provide additional guidance on selecting courses, navigating policies and degree requirements, preparing for future employment, and exploring professional pathways. Expectations All candidates for coterminal master’s programs in Earth Systems (MS and MA) must secure an academic advisor before applying to the coterm program. Coterm advisors must be members of the Academic Council. Each student is expected to meet with their advisor at least once per quarter to discuss degree progress and new course selections. Students must obtain their advisor’s signed approval on their course plan each quarter, as courses taken may differ from the original course plan submitted with the coterm application. The final curriculum must stay true to the scope and rigor of the initially approved curriculum, even if some of the individual courses change. Because Earth Systems is an interdisciplinary program with no faculty, the program relies upon faculty in related departments to advise its students. This is particularly important for coterm students who are embarking on advanced studies and need the expertise of their advisors for curriculum planning and academic development. The program greatly appreciates this advising support, and the Earth Systems staff is available for any questions and to help however we can. Review: Coterm Advisor Guidelines. See the Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.
value.cotermTransferPolicy: After accepting admission to this coterminal master’s degree program, students may request a transfer of courses from the undergraduate to the graduate career to satisfy the requirements for the master’s degree. Transferring courses to the graduate career requires review and approval of both the undergraduate and graduate programs on a case-by-case basis. In this master’s program, courses taken during or after the first quarter of the sophomore year are eligible for consideration for transfer to the graduate career; the timing of the first graduate quarter is not a factor. No courses taken before the first quarter of the sophomore year may be used to meet master’s degree requirements. Course transfers are not possible after the bachelor’s degree has been conferred.
value.programGradingPolicies: All courses for the master’s program must be taken for a letter grade; courses not taken for a letter grade must be approved by the master’s advisor and Director of Earth Systems.
value.programGPARequirement: A minimum overall GPA of 3.4 must be maintained.
value.programAdditionalPolicies: Prerequisite courses may not be counted toward the 45 required MS units. Completion of prerequisite courses is not required prior to applying to the coterm program; however, all prerequisite courses must be completed prior to graduation. Students may petition to have alternative courses satisfy pre-requisite courses listed in the "Pre-requisite Coursework" section below.

value.A3i6E: The Emmett Interdisciplinary Program in Environment and Resources develops the knowledge, skills, perspectives, and ways of thinking to understand and help solve the world’s most significant environmental and resource sustainability challenges. E-IPER strives to be a model for interdisciplinary graduate education. E-IPER offers the following degrees: a PhD in Environment and Resources; a Joint MS for MBA students in Stanford’s Graduate School of Business or JD students in the Stanford Law School; and a Dual MS for master’s students across Stanford’s seven schools, MD students in the School of Medicine, or for PhD students in another department. E-IPER’s home is the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, and affiliated faculty come from all seven Stanford schools.
value.WOZxr: The E-IPER Joint and Dual MS program does not accept external credit (transfer credit or otherwise) toward degree completion. All coursework must be met and completed through the university’s offerings, including the university’s professional schools.
value.ItCSB: Completing the PhD and MS degrees in Environment and Resources provides students with the knowledge, skills, perspectives, and ways of thinking to understand and help solve the world’s most significant environmental and resource sustainability challenges.
value.advisingExpectations: The Emmett Interdisciplinary Program in Environment and Resources is committed to providing academic advising to support graduate students’ scholarly and professional development. Through the open discussions of scholarly ideas during regular interactions with their advisors, graduate students identify focus areas and develop their creative and intellectual potential more generally. Faculty advisors guide students in designing and conducting research, selecting courses, exploring academic opportunities and professional pathways, developing teaching skills, and navigating policies and degree requirements. At the same time, they are aware and respectful of work-life balance and wellness considerations. Graduate students proactively seek academic and professional guidance and take responsibility for learning about their program’s policies and degree requirements. Students should also take advantage of the more extensive advising network, consulting such resources as the E-IPER program staff, Stanford’s institutional resources (VPGE, Office of Graduate Life, CAPS, etc.), and individuals and networks in the broader community of scholars. While student academic progress is reviewed annually, students are expected to actively track their progress and raise concerns promptly. If students have a formal concern or complaint about their advising experience, they are encouraged to contact the E-IPER Associate Directors or the E-IPER Faculty Director. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising.

value.A3i6E: The purpose of the master’s program in Earth and Planetary Sciences is to continue a student’s training in a broad range of earth science disciplines and prepare students for either a professional career or doctoral studies.
value.WOZxr: Master’s degree students are not eligible for transfer residency credit. Students enrolled at Stanford who plan to study elsewhere during their degree program should, before their departure, obtain prior approval for any transfer residency they seek.
value.ItCSB: The MS is conferred upon candidates who have demonstrated substantial scholarship, high attainment in a particular field of knowledge, and the ability to conduct independent research. To this end, the program’s objectives are to enable students to develop the skills needed to conduct original investigations in a particular discipline or set of disciplines in the Earth and Planetary Sciences, to interpret the results, and to present the data and conclusions in a publishable manner. Inclusivity and Diversity The Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences strives to ensure that graduate students feel safe, secure, and supported during their graduate experience. It does not tolerate harassment targeting race, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, physical and mental ability, physical appearance, age, and/or religion. Any experience of discrimination, harassment, or inequity in the department will not be tolerated and will be met with appropriate consequences by Stanford University’s Harassment and Discrimination policy. Students can seek support from the Director of Access/Belonging, Erik Sperling , or the Assistant Director of Student Services, Anjani Varma . Mental Health Members of the Earth and Planetary Sciences department recognize that mental health challenges are real and can arise from both within and beyond the academic setting. We support and encourage each other to seek mental health and well-being resources. If any event during the graduate experience places a student under undue stress that inhibits their performance to their potential, the department encourages the student to seek support from the Director of Graduate Studies, Jane Willenbring , Assistant Director of Student Services Anjani Varma , or university services such as Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) or Graduate Life Office (GLO). Academic Accommodations The Office of Accessible Education (OAE) is the campus office designated to work with Stanford students with disabilities. To comply with Stanford’s academic accommodations process, faculty should not attempt to arrange accommodations with the student. Students with questions about accommodations should contact OAE to initiate a disability-related request for accommodations. When a student presents an OAE Accommodation Letter, that letter should be followed, or the faculty member should work with the student and OAE to implement and/or modify the recommended accommodations. Students are expected to initiate accommodation requests promptly and provide timely notification of changes to approved accommodations. Faculty are responsible for maintaining student confidentiality and treating all disability-related information as confidential.
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences is committed to providing academic advising to support graduate students’ scholarly and professional development. The department strives to ensure everyone has a fulfilling experience by creating an inclusive culture. The Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability shares this commitment as reflected in the Doerr School Policy on Respectful and Inclusive Behavior. The advising relationship entails collaborative and sustained engagement by both the advisor and the advisee. Both the advisor and the advisee are expected to maintain professionalism and integrity. Establishing Advisor-Advisee Expectations Both advisor and advisee are expected to take responsibility for actively discussing the nature of the graduate experience. For first-year students, the discussion results on the nature of the graduate experience and each party's expectations are summarized in a document that both the advisor and the advisee sign. The relationship and expectations evolve as the student progresses through their graduate experience. Regularly scheduled advisor-advisee interactions are an essential component of this relationship. Advisors are expected to check in with their students every quarter to discuss how expectations are being met and whether any need updating. Students are encouraged to revisit these conversations when the advisor-advisee relationship is not meeting their needs or expectations. Additionally, a written review in the spring quarter covers the student’s academic progress with their advisor(s) and committee members. Graduate students are expected to proactively seek academic and professional guidance and take responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for their graduate program. In addition to the primary advisor, students are highly encouraged to seek advice from other faculty in the department and other faculty and researchers (Stanford or external) who align with their research interests. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. Students can seek support and assistance from the Assistant Director of Student Services Anjani Varma when needed. Guidelines for advisor-advisee interactions The advisor-advisee relationship is mutual. Graduate students and faculty can expect mutual respect, high professional standards, and the sharing of ideas and research. Advisors should strive continuously to improve their mentoring abilities. Group dynamics can be complex; advisors should strive to treat students equitably, including the distribution of opportunities in a group, classroom, field, and laboratory settings. Further information regarding guidelines and best practices for advising and mentoring is available from the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education. Graduate students are expected to exercise high professional standards in their academic work, research, and mentoring partnerships and to be proactive in seeking advice and keeping the advisor informed about academic and research progress. Our program unites basic and purpose-driven research to understand how the Earth functions, the many ways it is changing, and what the consequences of these changes will be for people and other species. We train students to understand, predict, and respond to human-caused and natural environmental change at local to global scales. value.A3i6E: The MS in Energy Science and Engineering prepares students for professional careers in the energy and engineering sectors, as well as in related technical fields. The program develops a broad set of skills, including a strong foundation in physical principles, data analysis, computational methods, and system-level understanding of complex energy systems. It may also serve as a pathway to a PhD for those interested in research or academic careers. The MS program is offered both as a standalone degree and as a coterminal option for Stanford undergraduates. The coterminal program allows students to begin graduate-level coursework while completing their BS. Standalone MS Program in Energy Science and Engineering The MS program in Energy Science and Engineering offers two degree options: a research-based degree, and a coursework-only degree. The requirements for each option, including required coursework, are described below. The program can take up to two years to complete. Coterminal MS Program in Energy Science and Engineering The coterminal BS/MS program allows Stanford undergraduates to pursue a master’s degree in Energy Science and Engineering while completing a BS in a related field. Students commonly enter the program from backgrounds such as chemical, civil, or mechanical engineering, earth sciences, physics, or chemistry. Coterminal students must meet all master’s degree requirements described in this bulletin, as well as university policies outlined in the Coterminal Master’s Program and Graduate Degrees sections. After admission to the coterminal program, students may request to transfer eligible undergraduate coursework to their graduate record to fulfill MS degree requirements. These requests are reviewed and approved on a case-by-case basis by both the undergraduate and graduate programs. The university requires that a graduate advisor be assigned in the student’s first graduate quarter, even if the undergraduate career remains active. In addition, the student must complete and obtain departmental approval of the Master’s Degree Program Proposal by the end of that same quarter.
value.ItCSB: The MS program in Energy Science and Engineering prepares students to become technical leaders in the energy sector, academia, and research organizations. Graduates of the program are expected to: Apply fundamental principles from engineering and related sciences to analyze and solve energy-related problems Formulate, analyze, and synthesize solutions to contemporary and emerging challenges in energy systems Work effectively both independently and collaboratively to develop and improve engineering solutions Communicate technical concepts and results clearly through written, visual, and oral formats Demonstrate an advanced and integrated understanding of energy systems and technologies Students pursuing the research-based MS degree are additionally expected to: Conduct a rigorous and original scientific investigation that addresses a significant and well-defined research problem
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Energy Science and Engineering is committed to providing high-quality academic advising to support MS students in their educational and professional development. At or before the start of graduate study (generally at the beginning of autumn quarter) each student is assigned an advisor: a member of our faculty who provides research guidance and advice on course selection, academic opportunities, and professional pathways. A key early milestone is the MS Program Proposal, which each student completes at the end of their first quarter. Research-track MS students meet regularly with their advisor, both one-on-one and as part of their research group. When meetings are not feasible, students are expected to stay in touch through other means, such as emailing brief progress updates. Students are also expected to meet with their advisor during or before the first week of each quarter to agree on the courses they plan to take. Advisors formally approve the study list in person or by email. The Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) meets with all MS students at the start of their first year and is available throughout the academic year by email and during office hours. The department's student services office is also an integral part of the advising framework: it informs students and advisors about university and departmental requirements, procedures, and opportunities, and maintains official records of advising assignments and approvals. Students are encouraged to consult both the DGS and the student services office for guidance in working with their advisor. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. Requests must be submitted to the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS) and are subject to review and approval by the Graduate Standing Committee. Students who are not in good academic standing are not eligible to request a change. For students in good standing, approval depends on alignment with program requirements and faculty availability.

The program spans scales from subsurface processes, such as fluid flow and energy transport in geologic formations, to surface systems involving energy conversion, storage, transmission, and utilization. These foundations support applications including geothermal and hydrocarbon energy recovery, CO₂ sequestration, battery and hydrogen energy storage, and groundwater remediation. Graduates are prepared to develop innovative, system-level solutions for a sustainable and resilient energy future.

value.programAdditionalPolicies: PhD Minor in Another Department The student must propose the possibility of pursuing a PhD minor, clearly and explicitly, in the written PhD proposal. value.A3i6E: Environmental Social Sciences (ESoS) is a new department within the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. The following program guidelines provide a starting point for the new department. Iterations on this foundation will be forthcoming. The PhD is a research degree. Teaching students to conduct high-quality independent research is thus a primary objective of the ESoS graduate program. Carrying out and publishing such research as a graduate student, in addition to its central pedagogical role, has also become a prerequisite for obtaining professional positions. As such, our graduate program is structured to encourage research, and the development of research skills, to the maximum extent possible. The ESoS PhD program follows a cohort model, admitting students to the department and not tying student funding to a specific faculty member. This approach allows students and faculty to find advisor matches that work for both and to transfer advisors if necessary. The ESoS department includes two faculty groups: Environmental Behavioral Sciences (EBS) and Global Environmental Policy (GEP). The ESoS PhD program runs with independent EBS and GEP subplans. Students apply and are admitted to a specific subplan. EBS and GEP subplans have different advisors and subplan-specific expectations, including course requirements.
value.WOZxr: Students may receive credit for previous courses subject to approval by the DGS in their subplan.
value.ItCSB: ESoS PhD graduates will be able to demonstrate competence in qualitative and quantitative methodologies in the behavioral and social sciences by applying them to original research in environmental topics. They will develop data science skills to be able to work with complex workflows, large data, and/or spatial data science. Students in both subplans will be trained to design and execute rigorous research that advances scientific understanding and impacts policy. We expect that the quantitative learning objectives will be achieved largely through methods coursework and that the topical and institutional knowledge objectives will be achieved through topical depth requirements. EBS subplan graduates will demonstrate competence in natural and social scientific theories. They will demonstrate epistemological fluency across a range of environmental social sciences theories and methodological approaches, and they will be able to critically evaluate and deploy these frameworks in context-appropriate ways that maintain coherence between the underlying ontological assumptions and epistemological commitments. GEP subplan graduates will use and evaluate methodologies and approaches from multiple quantitative social sciences, natural science, and computer science. They will apply knowledge of the policies and institutions that shape environmental outcomes to evaluate and/or address complex sustainability problems.
value.advisingExpectations: EBS Subplan: Upon admission to the Environmental Behavioral Sciences (EBS) subplan in the Environmental Social Sciences PhD program, students initially will be supported by the DGS and the Graduate Studies Committee (GSC). In a matching process completed by the end of Winter Quarter first year, students will work with the DGS and GSC to identify their advising team: an advisor or co-advisors and one or two additional EBS faculty members. At that point, the advisory relationship is passed from the DGS/GSC to the advisor(s) and committee member(s) who will work with the student to develop the Graduate Research Plan, as well as provide ongoing guidance in course selection and research. Mentored research should begin in June, after completion of the first year of coursework. Throughout the PhD program, students will receive ongoing support from the DGS and the GSC, including participating in an annual meeting to review programmatic progress. Additionally, students will be encouraged to develop mentoring and working relationships across the EBS faculty through formal and informal pathways including, but not limited to, courses, WEBS, the EBS seminar, and participation in lab/faculty groups. GEP Subplan: Throughout the Global Environmental Policy (GEP) subplan in the Environmental Social Sciences PhD program, students will receive advising from: a primary academic advisor within GEP an optional secondary academic advisor within GEP or other appropriate department a non-academic mentor within GEP (not a committee member) students are encouraged to obtain a committee member from outside GEP in natural sciences, engineering, or related non-social-science field Students will develop their academic and research plans in coordination with their academic advisors and the Director of Graduate Studies (DGS). The non-academic mentor is not involved with the student’s research and is designated to support a student’s career development as well as their mental, physical, and emotional well-being. Students will meet with the DGS annually to review their progress in the program. Advisor assignment and selection: After students are admitted to the GEP subplan but before beginning the program in fall quarter, they will be assigned two initial advisors by the DGS. Students will select a primary and possible secondary academic advisor within GEP during their first year. Students will inform the DGS when they have identified a permanent GEP advisor(s) and will transition to developing a research plan with their permanent advisor(s). Mentored research should begin in June, after completion of their first year of coursework. Handling Concerns/Conflicts: As part of their advising network, students are encouraged to consult departmental resources (such as department and school student services staff, the thesis committee, the EBS/GEP Directors of Graduate Studies, and the department Chair), Stanford institutional resources (such as the VPGE, the Office of Graduate Life, CAPS, and the campus Ombuds), as well as individuals and networks in the broader scientific community. In the event that a student has a formal concern or complaint about their advising experience, they are encouraged to contact the EBS/GEP Directors of Graduate Studies, the department Chair, the SDSS Assistant Dean for Student and Postdoctoral Affairs, and/or the SDSS Associate Dean for Human Resources and Faculty Affairs. In the event that either the student or advisor feels that the advising relationship is not effective, the school process for formally evaluating student/advisor assignments may be activated. This typically begins with speaking with the Director of Graduate Studies, who can then inform the student/advisor about appropriate next steps.
value.programGradingPolicies: All courses taken for the program must be completed with a letter grade, if the course is offered for a letter grade.
value.programGPARequirement: Students must maintain at least a 3.0 grade point average.
value.programAdditionalPolicies: ESoS PhD students must register for 8-10 units per quarter and 3 units during the summer quarter, unless otherwise required by the program. Students must pass at least 6 units per quarter. Time to Completion of Degree: The departmental PhD should be accomplished within five years. To achieve this, students, together with their advisor(s) and committee members, need to set realistic milestones throughout a student’s graduate program. Extension to a sixth year will be considered, but only due to extenuating circumstances. Residency Requirements: Per university regulations, graduate students are expected to maintain a significant physical presence on the campus where their main advisor(s) is based, unless the degree program has granted an exception (for example, to conduct field work). This applies to each quarter a student is enrolled. Funding: PhD students in good standing will be funded for five academic years, consistent with the funding policies of the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability (SDSS). Funding past five years is not guaranteed. Professional Development: Environmental Social Sciences students will be offered occasional seminars and workshops to help navigate their time in graduate school and prepare for careers beyond it. Topics of these seminars will include, but not be limited to: orientation to Stanford and departmental resources, professionalism, scholarship, scientific ethics, well-being and mental health, service, career paths, navigating interpersonal relationships in academia and other professional environments, working in teams, open science, leadership, and effective practices for mentor-mentee relationships. Departmental/School Service: Graduate students in the Department of Environmental Social Sciences are expected to be active community members. This includes, but is not limited to, serving on ESoS, SDSS, and university committees as well as dedicating time to department, SDSS, and university-wide events. Graduate students are, first and foremost, students and thus expected to prioritize their scholarship and academics; thus, they should discuss with their advisor(s) the appropriate amount of time and effort dedicated to service-related engagements.

value.A3i6E: Geophysics is a hybrid discipline uniquely devoted to applying physical principles and methods to studying Earth’s and other planets’ complex systems (processes and properties). The undergraduate and graduate programs are designed to provide a background of fundamentals in science and courses to coordinate these fundamentals with the principles of geophysics. Graduate programs offer specialized training for professional work in resource exploration, research, and education and lead to the degrees of Master of Science and Doctor of Philosophy. Graduate Degrees describes university requirements for the MS and PhD. The MS program is available either as a standalone MS degree or as a coterminal degree.
value.ItCSB: The graduate program in Geophysics aims to prepare students to be leaders in the geophysics industry, academia, and research organizations through the completion of fundamental courses in their major field and related sciences and through independent research. Students are expected to: Apply skills developed in fundamental courses to geophysical problems Research, analyze, and synthesize solutions to an original and contemporary geophysics problem Work independently and as part of a team to develop and improve geophysics solutions Apply written, visual, and oral presentation skills to communicate scientific knowledge An in-depth technical understanding of geophysics problems at an advanced level (master’s students) Complete a scientific investigation that is significant, challenging, and original (doctoral students)
value.advisingExpectations: The Department of Geophysics is committed to providing academic advising in support of graduate student scholarly and professional development. See Graduate Advising for a statement of university policy on graduate advising. Minimum Advising Expectations for the Department of Geophysics Each advisor meets with each advisee annually in autumn quarter to develop/update the Geophysics Graduate Advising Expectations Agreement that records the agreed-upon approach to the following for each advisee: Courses: the process and responsibility for selecting courses Thesis topic: the process and responsibility for choosing the topic Members of advising committee: the process and responsibility for the selection Meetings of advisor and advisee: structure and frequency Conducting the research: the level of independence and progress expected, the involvement of the advisor (level of participation, nature of oversight), involvement of other collaborators (both inside and outside of the research group) Thesis content, including expectations concerning publications Writing of publications: style of interaction, policy on co-authorship, publication costs Conference travel/presentations: who attends/presents, frequency, financial support Funding (stipend, tuition, research costs): source, responsibilities, requirements for ongoing support In-the-office hours Vacations and other absences Expectations for summer quarter Preparing for career interests, and plans after Stanford The document, signed by the advisor and advisee, is submitted to the assistant director of student services. If the advisor-advisee discussion would benefit from the involvement of an additional person, either the advisor or advisee can request the presence of a faculty or staff member of the school. The expectations agreement is reviewed by the assistant director of student services and the director of graduate studies, with follow-up as needed. If there is a change in advisor, the expectations agreement must be completed with the new advisor within the first quarter after the change. 2. A one-hour annual review focused on academic progress is held every year; in the first year, this is deferred to autumn of the second year. This meeting includes the advisee and the advising committee [see below details on committee composition]. At any time, a student with questions or concerns can approach any one of the following individuals in the school: Other faculty members of the advisory committee Assistant director of student services Director of graduate studies Director of diversity and inclusion Department chair Alyssa Ferree, Assistant Dean of Student and Postdoctoral Affairs Jenny Saltzman, Assistant Dean for Professional Development and Community Sue Crutcher, Associate Dean for Human Resources and Faculty Affairs Faculty Advisor Students admitted to the Geophysics MS program are assigned a faculty advisor. This faculty advisor carries out the responsibilities described in the Graduate Academic Policy and Procedures (GAP) handbook. The faculty advisor is also responsible for other aspects of mentoring students during their time at Stanford, including monitoring academic progress. This faculty advisor is a member of the Academic Council with a primary or joint appointment in the Geophysics Department; this does not include courtesy or adjunct faculty. Faculty who have recently become emeritus and have been recalled to active duty may serve as Faculty Advisor, even though they are no longer current members of the Academic Council. More information about the role of the faculty advisor and the university academic advising policies can be found in the GAP handbook . In the exceptional case where permission is granted by the chair for a student to have a faculty advisor outside the Geophysics department, it is recommended (but not required) that the student have a co-advisor within the Geophysics department. Advising Committee The Geophysics department requires each MS student to have an advising committee formed by the student and advisor before the student’s first annual review (typically autumn quarter of the second year). The advising committee provides additional support and expertise for the MS student as they conduct their research. The advising committee includes the faculty advisor and (if relevant) the co-advisor, plus at least one other Stanford faculty member (members of the Stanford Academic Council or emeriti faculty). The advising committee can also include a committee member (from inside or outside of Stanford) that contributes to an area of expertise that is not readily available from the faculty and holds a PhD or equivalent foreign degree. If a faculty member on an advising committee is on sabbatical or leave, they will have either agreed to continue serving in an advisory capacity or will have made an alternate arrangement. Students should discuss this with the faculty member and can consult with their faculty advisor or the director of graduate studies. Process for Addressing Concerns Related to Advisor/Advisee Relationship: Faculty members with academic concerns about their advisees can contact the assistant director of student services(ADSS) to discuss options. Dismissal of graduate students is addressed in separate guidelines (see GAP 5.6 Dismissal For Academic and Professional Reasons ). The following are examples of options to address academic and/or wellbeing concerns of graduate students: Consultation with members of the advising committee, director of graduate studies (DGS), director of diversity and inclusion (DDI) or department chair Consultation with university support offices including the dean’s office, the Graduate Life Office (GLO), Bechtel International Center , the Office of Accessible Education (OAE), Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS), and the Ombuds office. Students with concerns about the advisee/advisor relationship should meet with the ADSS to discuss options. The ADSS will provide resources as well as recommend that the student meet with a faculty member (such as a member of their advisory committee, the DGS, the DDI, department chair or any faculty member to whom they feel comfortable speaking). In cases where the advisor/advisee relationship does not improve, the student will be supported in developing and implementing a formal, agreed-upon plan to correct the situation. The steps for doing so are as follows: The student meets with the ADSS again to review concerns and clearly document examples of the concerns as well as attempts made to mediate the concerns. The student meets with the DGS and/or the department chair and if appropriate the ADSS will join the meetings. The student may consult with Graduate Life Office for additional support. Following the series of meetings with appropriate support staff and faculty, and assessment of concerns, the student, in consultation with the support staff and any faculty, creates a draft advising plan with goals, concerns, ideas for solutions, timelines, any other pertinent information (such as increased 1:1 advising, team advising, a timeline for check-ins, etc.). The draft advising plan must also include a schedule for check-in meetings with the ADSS, DGS, or other relevant people, no less than once per quarter, to ensure that the plan has been successful. The draft advising plan, along with the student’s Advising Expectations document, is shared in advance of the meeting that is detailed next. A meeting is organized with the DGS, advisor, student, ADSS, and any other faculty (such as the chair of the department where the advisor has their primary appointment) or support staff (such as a GLO dean or the university ombuds) that the DGS or student would like to have in attendance. The meeting is chaired by the DGS. The student presents the advising plan and all members of the meeting discuss the plan. At the conclusion of the meeting, the advising plan is updated to reflect any changes agreed upon during the meeting. The updated advising plan is approved by the student, advisor, and the DGS, and placed in the student’s file by the ADSS. Following the meeting, the student follows the check-in process described in the advising plan. Should students request more information about changing advisors, they should read the school policy as well as speak to both the ADSS and DGS or appropriate faculty members. SDSS Intranet Login

The plan sets specific and measurable objectives that must be met over a reasonable time period determined by the Advisor. The time period is at least one quarter but no more than one academic year. This plan is captured in a document that is signed off by the student, the student’s Advisor, and the DGS. value.ItCSB: The objectives of the doctoral program in Oceans are to enable students to develop the skills needed to conduct interdisciplinary, collaborative and original investigations into oceans-related research to advance exploration and knowledge of our blue planet and tackle the most pressing challenges in climate and sustainability. Graduates must also be able to interpret research results and present the data and conclusions in a publishable manner while developing strong teaching and effective public-facing communication skills. We anticipate that our students will pursue various careers in academia, public and private sectors, including government labs, NGOs, and state and local governments.
value.advisingExpectations: Upon entering the program, students along with their Primary Advisor will choose a First Year Advisory Committee, consisting of the student’s primary advisor and 1-2 other faculty members who align with the student’s scientific interests. Students will be encouraged to meet with members of this committee throughout the first year to request further guidance on these topics. Graduate students are active contributors to the advising relationship. They should proactively seek academic and professional guidance and take responsibility for informing themselves of policies and degree requirements for the Oceans PhD program. value.programGradingPolicies: If offered, any course that satisfies the PhD degree requirements must be taken for a letter grade.
value.programGPARequirement: A minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0 or above is required for all courses. An overall grade point average (GPA) of at least 3.0 must be maintained.
value.programAdditionalPolicies: All students in the PhD program are required to register autumn, winter, spring and summer quarters.
